questions.stem: A nurse is preparing an insulin infusion. A second nurse is available. What constitutes a correct independent double check?

options.text: The second nurse confirms the first nurse's calculation after seeing it
options.rationale: Near miss concept Being shown the answer defeats independence.

options.text: The second nurse watches the first nurse program the pump and agrees
options.rationale: Near miss concept Observation, not independent verification.

options.text: The second nurse signs the record once the infusion has been started
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting A signature after the fact checks nothing.

options.text: The second nurse checks order, drug, concentration and pump independently
options.rationale: Independent is the whole point. If the second nurse is shown the answer first, that nurse is checking agreement rather than accuracy, and confirmation bias makes that nurse far more likely to miss the same error. The second nurse reads the order independently, does the math independently, and then they compare. Watching and cosigning afterward are not checks at all.

questions.takeaway: If you tell the second nurse your answer first, you have not had a double check.
questions.strategy: Three options all involve the second nurse seeing the first nurse's work before doing their own check.

questions.stem: An 82 year old is scheduled for metoprolol 50 mg PO daily. Blood pressure is 88/52 and heart rate is 54. What should the nurse do?

options.rationale: Metoprolol lowers both heart rate and blood pressure, and both are already low in an older adult. The nurse holds, notifies the provider, documents and reassesses.

options.rationale: Near miss concept Memory is not verification; an unattended, unlabeled syringe is unsafe.

questions.takeaway: Unlabeled syringe: discard.

questions.strategy: Convert hours to minutes first.

questions.stem: A bag has 750 mL remaining and is infusing at 50 mL/hr. How many hours until it is empty?

options.text: 15 hours
options.rationale: Hours = volume / rate = 750 mL / 50 mL/hr = 15 hours.

options.text: 37.5 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept That multiplies instead of dividing.

options.text: 7.5 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept That divides by 100.

options.text: 12 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept That would hold only 600 mL.

questions.takeaway: Time = volume over rate.
questions.strategy: Set it up with units, cancel them, then ask whether the answer makes sense.

options.text: 625 mL
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is 5 hours.

options.text: 750 mL
options.rationale: Volume = rate x time = 125 mL/hr x 6 hr = 750 mL.

options.text: 800 mL
options.rationale: Near miss concept That does not match 125 x 6.

questions.strategy: Set it up with units, cancel them, then ask whether the answer makes sense.

questions.stem: A nurse calculates that an oral dose requires 12 tablets. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give 6 tablets now and 6 tablets in an hour
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Splitting the dose changes the order.

options.text: Ask the patient how many tablets are usually taken
options.rationale: Near miss concept The patient is not the source for verifying a calculation.

options.text: Give the 12 tablets, since the math was checked once
options.rationale: Near miss concept An unreasonable answer needs a second check.

options.text: Recheck the calculation and the order before giving anything
options.rationale: An answer far outside what is usual signals an error in the setup, the units or the order. The nurse rechecks and clarifies, and does not give a dose that looks wrong.

questions.takeaway: If it looks wrong, it probably is.
questions.strategy: Compare the answer with an estimate.

questions.stem: Which oral form is usually absorbed fastest?

options.text: A liquid solution
options.rationale: Liquids are already dissolved, so they are absorbed faster, usually in the stomach. Tablets and capsules must break down first.

options.text: A film coated tablet
options.rationale: Near miss concept A tablet must dissolve first, so it is slower than a liquid.

options.text: An enteric coated tablet
options.rationale: Near miss concept Enteric coating delays absorption until the intestine.

options.text: An extended release capsule
options.rationale: Near miss concept Extended release forms absorb slowly by design.

questions.takeaway: Liquid is fastest.
questions.strategy: The fewer steps before absorption, the faster.

questions.stem: Why is an enteric coated tablet never crushed or split?

options.text: The coating makes the tablet easier to swallow
options.rationale: Near miss concept Easier swallowing is not the coating's purpose.

options.text: Splitting it changes the drug into a different form
options.rationale: Near miss concept The drug stays the same; it is released in the wrong place.

options.text: The coating protects the stomach lining from the drug
options.rationale: Enteric coating keeps the tablet intact in the stomach so it dissolves in the intestine. Crushing it exposes the stomach lining to irritation and can destroy acid sensitive drugs.

options.text: Crushing it makes the drug taste bitter
options.rationale: Near miss concept Taste is not the reason for the rule.

questions.takeaway: Enteric coated: whole, never crushed.
questions.strategy: Ask what the coating protects.

questions.stem: A nurse gives oral medications. Select all of the instructions the nurse gives the assistive personnel.

options.text: Crush any tablet the patient cannot swallow
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Preparing medications is not delegated.

options.text: Report coughing or choking during meals
options.rationale: Administering medications is not delegated to AP. The nurse tells the AP what side effects to watch for and to report changes in the patient's condition.

options.text: Hand the patient the pills left at the bedside
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Medications are never left at the bedside for AP to give.

options.text: Report any side effects you notice
options.rationale: Administering medications is not delegated to AP. The nurse tells the AP what side effects to watch for and to report changes in the patient's condition.

options.text: Give the next dose if the patient asks
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope AP cannot administer medications.

options.text: Tell me if the patient's condition changes
options.rationale: Administering medications is not delegated to AP. The nurse tells the AP what side effects to watch for and to report changes in the patient's condition.

questions.takeaway: AP observe and report; they do not give medications.
questions.strategy: Separate observing from administering.

questions.stem: Place the three safety checks for oral medications in order.

options.text: At the bedside, comparing with the MAR before giving
When removing the medication from the dispensing cabinet
Before entering the room, comparing the medication with the MAR

questions.takeaway: The label is compared with the medication administration record (MAR) when removing it, before entering the room and at the bedside before giving it. Remove, before the room, bedside.
questions.strategy: Follow the drug from the cabinet to the patient.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct practices for giving medications through a feeding tube.

options.text: Mix all medications together to save time
options.rationale: Near miss concept Each medication is given separately with flushes between.

options.text: Consult pharmacy before crushing a tablet
options.rationale: Liquids are preferred. Pharmacy confirms whether a tablet can be crushed. Placement is verified first, and the enteral connector prevents a wrong route connection.

options.text: Use the enteral connector, not an IV syringe
options.rationale: Liquids are preferred. Pharmacy confirms whether a tablet can be crushed. Placement is verified first, and the enteral connector prevents a wrong route connection.

options.text: Use liquid forms when available
options.rationale: Liquids are preferred. Pharmacy confirms whether a tablet can be crushed. Placement is verified first, and the enteral connector prevents a wrong route connection.

options.text: Give enteric coated tablets crushed in water
options.rationale: Near miss concept Enteric coated tablets are not crushed.

options.text: Verify tube placement before giving anything
options.rationale: Liquids are preferred. Pharmacy confirms whether a tablet can be crushed. Placement is verified first, and the enteral connector prevents a wrong route connection.

questions.takeaway: Liquid, check pharmacy, verify placement, enteral connector.
questions.strategy: Reject shortcuts that combine or crush.

questions.stem: Complete the instruction the nurse gives the assistive personnel after medications through a feeding tube.
questions.sentence: Keep the head of the bed at least [[1]] for [[2]] after the medications, and report [[3]] right away.

30 degrees
90 degrees
1 hour

a bowel movement

questions.takeaway: Keeping the head of the bed at least 30 degrees for 1 hour after tube medications reduces aspiration. Coughing, choking, gagging or drooling of liquid are reported immediately. 30 degrees for 1 hour, report choking.
questions.strategy: Every instruction prevents aspiration.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do before applying the next dose of a topical cream?

options.text: Cover the old dose with a dressing first
options.rationale: Near miss concept AP and nurses do not cover topical drugs unless ordered.

options.text: Warm the cream in the microwave
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heating changes the drug and can burn the skin.

options.text: Apply it over the previous dose
options.rationale: Near miss concept New medication is never layered over the old dose.

options.text: Clean the skin of the old medication first
options.rationale: Old medication is cleaned off so the dose is accurate and the skin can be assessed. Layering doses can increase absorption and cause systemic effects.

questions.takeaway: Clean first, never layer.
questions.strategy: Ask how the nurse knows the dose is correct.

questions.stem: What should the nurse tell the assistive personnel to expect after eye drops are given?

options.text: Ringing in the ears
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ringing in the ears is not an eye drop effect.

options.text: Temporary burning or blurred vision
options.rationale: Eye medications commonly cause brief burning or blurring. The AP knows this is expected and reports other side effects.

options.text: Permanent changes in vision
options.rationale: Near miss concept Expected effects are temporary.

options.text: A drop in blood glucose
options.rationale: Near miss concept Eye drops do not affect glucose.

questions.takeaway: Eye drops: brief burning or blur.
questions.strategy: Choose the local, temporary effect.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct practices for giving ear drops.

options.text: Insert the dropper tip into the ear canal to seal it
options.rationale: Near miss concept The dropper should not occlude the ear canal.

options.text: Use any drops left over from another patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept Medications are never shared between patients.

options.text: Use sterile drops in case the eardrum is ruptured
options.rationale: Room temperature drops prevent dizziness. Sterile drops protect a possibly ruptured eardrum. The dropper is not pushed into the canal.

options.text: Give cold drops to reduce swelling
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cold drops can cause dizziness and discomfort.

options.text: Tell the AP the patient may feel dizzy afterward
options.rationale: Room temperature drops prevent dizziness. Sterile drops protect a possibly ruptured eardrum. The dropper is not pushed into the canal.

options.text: Give the drops at room temperature
options.rationale: Room temperature drops prevent dizziness. Sterile drops protect a possibly ruptured eardrum. The dropper is not pushed into the canal.

questions.takeaway: Ear drops: room temperature, sterile, do not block the canal.
questions.strategy: Each correct practice prevents dizziness or infection.

questions.stem: A patient has trouble pressing the inhaler and breathing in at the same time. What does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Holding the inhaler upside down
options.rationale: Near miss concept Turning the inhaler upside down does not improve delivery.

options.text: A spacer or a breath actuated inhaler
options.rationale: A pressurized metered dose inhaler (MDI) needs coordination between pressing and inhaling. A spacer holds the mist, and a breath actuated inhaler fires when the patient breathes in.

options.text: A larger number of puffs per dose
options.rationale: Near miss concept More puffs do not fix poor technique.

options.text: Switching to oral tablets only
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing the route is the provider's decision and not needed.

questions.takeaway: Poor coordination: spacer or breath actuated inhaler.
questions.strategy: Fix the coordination problem.

questions.stem: Match each feature to the inhaler.

rows.text: Uses a propellant to spray the dose
May need a spacer if coordination is poor

questions.takeaway: An MDI uses a propellant to release a spray and needs coordination, so a spacer can help. A DPI holds dry powder, creates the aerosol when the patient inhales, has no propellant and needs no spacer. MDI: propellant, spacer. DPI: neither.
questions.strategy: Ask what makes the dose leave the device.

questions.stem: Select all of the practices that support patient centered medication teaching.

options.text: Give all teaching only in writing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Teaching is adapted to the patient's needs, including vision, hearing or cognition.

options.text: Avoid discussing cultural health beliefs
options.rationale: Near miss concept Health beliefs influence how patients use medications and must be explored.

options.text: Include family caregivers in teaching sessions
options.rationale: Culture, beliefs, herbal remedies and food choices affect adherence and interactions. Materials must match reading level and sensory needs, and caregivers are included.

options.text: Ask about food preferences that may interact with drugs
options.rationale: Culture, beliefs, herbal remedies and food choices affect adherence and interactions. Materials must match reading level and sensory needs, and caregivers are included.

options.text: Use print materials at an appropriate reading level
options.rationale: Culture, beliefs, herbal remedies and food choices affect adherence and interactions. Materials must match reading level and sensory needs, and caregivers are included.

options.text: Ask about herbal remedies and alternative therapies
options.rationale: Culture, beliefs, herbal remedies and food choices affect adherence and interactions. Materials must match reading level and sensory needs, and caregivers are included.

questions.takeaway: Teach to the person, not the pamphlet.
questions.strategy: Pick options that adapt to the patient.

questions.stem: Why can eye drops or a rectal medication cause effects throughout the body?

options.text: Mucous membranes are highly vascular and absorb drugs quickly
options.rationale: Membranes such as the cornea and rectal mucosa have a rich blood supply, so drugs absorb quickly and can reach the whole body.

options.text: The drugs are always given in large volumes
options.rationale: Near miss concept The volumes are small.

options.text: These routes bypass all of the blood vessels
options.rationale: Near miss concept The opposite is true; blood flow is what absorbs them.

options.text: The drugs are designed to be toxic in small amounts
options.rationale: Near miss concept They are not designed to be toxic.

questions.takeaway: Membranes absorb fast and can act systemically.
questions.strategy: Think about blood flow at the site.

questions.stem: A nurse is giving medications through a nasogastric tube. Which action is correct?

options.text: Withhold the feeding permanently once medications are started
options.rationale: Near miss concept Some drugs require holding the feed briefly; permanent is wrong.

options.text: Give each medication separately and flush with water between them
options.rationale: Drugs interact with each other and with the feeding formula in the syringe and in the tube, and a clogged tube means a replacement and another x ray. One at a time with a flush between, and flushes before and after the whole sequence. Enteric coated and extended release forms are never crushed, because crushing delivers the whole dose at once.

options.text: Crush the enteric coated tablet to fit through the tube
options.rationale: Near miss concept Destroys the coating and delivers the full dose at once.

options.text: Mix all the medications together and give them in one syringe
options.rationale: Near miss concept Interactions and clogging; the time saved costs a tube.

questions.takeaway: One drug, one flush. Never crush enteric coated or extended release.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options are the two fastest ways to clog a tube or overdose a patient.

questions.stem: A nurse is applying a new transdermal patch. Which action is correct?

options.text: Apply the new patch over the old one to keep drug levels steady
options.rationale: Near miss concept Doubles the dose, and this is a documented cause of death.

options.text: Remove the old patch, wear gloves, and record the new site and time
options.rationale: Old patches left on stack doses, and fentanyl deaths have been traced to exactly that. Gloves keep the drug off your own skin. Sites rotate to prevent irritation and changes in absorption. Most patches cannot be cut, because the reservoir or rate controlling membrane is destroyed and the whole dose dumps.

options.text: Cut the patch in half when a lower dose has been prescribed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Destroys the delivery system in most formulations.

options.text: Apply the patch to the same site each time for even absorption
options.rationale: Near miss concept Irritates the skin and changes absorption unpredictably.

questions.takeaway: Find the old patch before you put on a new one. Document where you put it.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option produces a dose the patient did not get ordered.

questions.stem: While giving medications through a nasogastric tube, a patient begins coughing, the respiratory rate rises to 28 and SpO2 falls from 96% to 89%. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop all medications and fluids through the tube
options.rationale: These are signs of aspiration. Stop everything through the tube, raise the head of the bed and stay with the patient, assessing vital signs and breath sounds while another staff member notifies the provider.

options.text: Flush the tube with 30 mL of water
options.rationale: Near miss concept More water worsens aspiration.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed to ease breathing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lowering the head increases aspiration.

options.text: Finish the remaining medications quickly
options.rationale: Near miss concept Continuing adds more fluid to the airway.

questions.takeaway: Suspected aspiration: stop, elevate, stay.
questions.strategy: Stop the cause before anything else.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes after a new oral antibiotic, a patient has itchy hives, a runny nose and new wheezing. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Give the next dose with food
options.rationale: Near miss concept Food does not prevent an allergic reaction.

options.text: Reassure the patient that hives are expected
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Hives and wheezing are not expected.

options.text: Document the allergy in the record
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The allergy is documented after the patient is assessed and safe.

options.text: Withhold further doses and assess vital signs
options.rationale: Urticaria, pruritus, rhinitis and wheezing suggest an allergic reaction that may need emergency drugs. The nurse withholds the drug, assesses vital signs, notifies the provider and pharmacy, then documents the allergy.

questions.takeaway: Allergy signs: withhold, assess, notify.
questions.strategy: Act before you chart.

questions.stem: After timolol eye drops, a patient reports dizziness. Heart rate is 48 and blood pressure is 92/56. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Rinse the eye with water and continue the schedule
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Rinsing does not address a systemic effect.

options.text: Dim the lights and recheck the heart rate again in an hour
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dimming lights helps local burning, not systemic effects.

options.text: Stay with the patient, assess vital signs and notify the provider
options.rationale: Eye drops can be absorbed systemically. A beta blocker eye drop can slow the heart and lower pressure. The nurse stays with the patient, assesses vital signs, withholds further doses and notifies the provider.

options.text: Give the next dose early to stabilize the effect
options.rationale: Near miss concept More drug worsens the effect.

questions.takeaway: Systemic effects from drops: stay, assess, withhold, notify.
questions.strategy: Separate local from systemic effects.

questions.stem: A patient using an albuterol inhaler reports being lightheaded and feels the heart racing and skipping. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give another puff to open the airway further
options.rationale: Near miss concept More drug worsens the dysrhythmia.

options.text: Withhold further doses and evaluate cardiac and lung status
options.rationale: Beta adrenergic bronchodilators can cause dysrhythmias. The nurse withholds further doses, evaluates cardiac and pulmonary status and notifies the provider to reassess the drug and delivery method.

options.text: Encourage the patient to walk to improve circulation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Activity increases cardiac demand.

options.text: Switch to the spacer and give the next dose
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question A spacer does not prevent cardiac effects.

questions.takeaway: Dysrhythmia after a bronchodilator: withhold and notify.
questions.strategy: Stop the drug causing the new problem.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma has needed albuterol every 2 hours today. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: A worsening respiratory problem that needs reassessment
options.rationale: Needing a bronchodilator more than every 4 hours may signal a worsening respiratory problem. The nurse reassesses the drug and delivery method and notifies the provider.

options.text: An expected need on the first day of use
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Needing a rescue inhaler more than every 4 hours is not expected.

options.text: The patient prefers the inhaler to oral drugs
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Preference does not explain frequent use.

options.text: The inhaler technique is perfect
options.rationale: Near miss concept Good technique would reduce the need, not increase it.

questions.takeaway: Rescue inhaler more than every 4 hours: report.
questions.strategy: Frequency of rescue use is a warning sign.

questions.stem: After a week of ear drops, a patient's hearing has not improved. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Notify the provider; cerumen may be impacted
options.rationale: If hearing does not improve, the nurse notifies the provider. Impacted cerumen may need irrigation.

options.text: Tell the patient hearing loss is permanent
options.rationale: Near miss concept No evidence supports permanence.

options.text: Insert a cotton swab to clear the canal
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cotton swabs push cerumen deeper.

options.text: Increase the number of drops per dose
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing the dose is not a nursing decision.

questions.takeaway: No improvement: notify; think cerumen.
questions.strategy: Report a treatment that is not working.

questions.stem: A patient going home with eye drops cannot describe the steps and has trouble squeezing the bottle. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the patient to skip doses that are difficult
options.rationale: Near miss concept Skipping doses is unsafe.

options.text: Give a printed handout with pictures of each step and end the teaching session
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome A handout does not show the patient can do the skill.

options.text: Document that teaching was completed
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Teaching is not complete if the patient cannot do it.

options.text: Repeat the teaching with the family caregiver and use return demonstration
options.rationale: The nurse repeats the instructions, includes the family caregiver and has the patient demonstrate the skill back.

questions.takeaway: Return demonstration proves the skill.
questions.strategy: Teaching ends when the patient can do it.

questions.stem: Match each injection route to its angle of insertion.
questions.takeaway: Intradermal injections enter just under the epidermis at 5 to 15 degrees. Subcutaneous injections go into fatty tissue at 45 to 90 degrees, depending on tissue and needle length. Intramuscular injections go straight in at 90 degrees. ID shallow, SQ 45 to 90, IM 90.
questions.strategy: Picture the tissue layer the needle must reach.

questions.stem: Match each use to the injection route.
questions.takeaway: Intradermal is for skin and allergy testing. Subcutaneous is for insulin, heparin and some vaccines. Intramuscular is for most vaccines, antibiotics and thicker medications. ID tests, SQ insulin and heparin, IM thick drugs and vaccines.
questions.strategy: Match the drug to the depth it needs.

questions.stem: Which needle has the smallest diameter?

options.text: 20 gauge
options.rationale: Near miss concept 20 gauge is larger than 25.

options.text: 22 gauge
options.rationale: Near miss concept 22 gauge is larger than 25.

options.text: 25 gauge
options.rationale: Gauge runs opposite to size: the higher the gauge number, the smaller the needle.

options.text: 18 gauge
options.rationale: Near miss concept 18 gauge is the largest of these.

questions.takeaway: Higher gauge, smaller needle.
questions.strategy: Gauge and diameter move in opposite directions.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about intradermal injections.
questions.sentence: An intradermal injection uses a [[1]] syringe, delivers [[2]] of medication and should raise [[3]] under the skin.

options.text: insulin
3 mL
tuberculin
1 to 2 mL

a deep lump

questions.takeaway: Intradermal injections use a 1 mL tuberculin syringe, deliver only 0.01 to 0.1 mL and form a small wheal, which shows the drug is in the dermis. ID: tuberculin syringe, tiny volume, wheal.
questions.strategy: Each blank is independent.

questions.stem: Select all of the recommended subcutaneous injection sites.

options.text: Outer aspect of the upper arm
options.rationale: The best subcutaneous sites are the outer upper arms, the abdomen from below the costal margins to the iliac crests and the anterior thighs.

options.text: Abdomen below the costal margins to the iliac crests
options.rationale: The best subcutaneous sites are the outer upper arms, the abdomen from below the costal margins to the iliac crests and the anterior thighs.

options.text: Over a bruised area
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bruised, scarred or inflamed areas are avoided.

options.text: Anterior thigh
options.rationale: The best subcutaneous sites are the outer upper arms, the abdomen from below the costal margins to the iliac crests and the anterior thighs.

options.text: Deltoid center for a deep injection
options.rationale: Near miss concept The deltoid muscle is an intramuscular site.

options.text: Ventrogluteal site
options.rationale: Near miss concept The ventrogluteal site is for intramuscular injections.

questions.takeaway: SQ: arm, belly, thigh.
questions.strategy: Separate fat sites from muscle sites.

questions.stem: When is the subcutaneous route avoided?

options.text: When the patient is receiving insulin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Insulin is commonly given subcutaneously.

options.text: When conditions impair blood flow to the tissue
options.rationale: Subcutaneous absorption depends on blood flow. Conditions that impair circulation, such as shock, make absorption unreliable.

options.text: When the medication volume is less than 1 mL
options.rationale: Near miss concept Small volumes are ideal for this route.

options.text: When the patient has adequate fatty tissue
options.rationale: Near miss concept Adequate tissue supports the route.

questions.takeaway: SQ needs blood flow.
questions.strategy: Absorption depends on perfusion.

questions.stem: Select all of the sites used for intramuscular injections.

options.text: Back of the upper arm fat
options.rationale: Near miss concept The fatty back of the arm is a subcutaneous site.

options.text: Deltoid
options.rationale: The intramuscular sites are the ventrogluteal, vastus lateralis and deltoid. The ventrogluteal site is preferred for adults because it avoids major nerves and vessels.

options.text: Vastus lateralis
options.rationale: The intramuscular sites are the ventrogluteal, vastus lateralis and deltoid. The ventrogluteal site is preferred for adults because it avoids major nerves and vessels.

options.text: Abdomen around the umbilicus
options.rationale: Near miss concept The abdomen is a subcutaneous site.

options.text: Inner forearm
options.rationale: Near miss concept The inner forearm is used for intradermal tests.

options.text: Ventrogluteal
options.rationale: The intramuscular sites are the ventrogluteal, vastus lateralis and deltoid. The ventrogluteal site is preferred for adults because it avoids major nerves and vessels.

questions.takeaway: IM: ventrogluteal, vastus lateralis, deltoid.
questions.strategy: Pick muscles, not fat.

questions.stem: How does the nurse locate the deltoid injection site?

options.text: At the elbow crease on the inner arm
options.rationale: Near miss concept The inner arm is not an IM site.

options.text: Over the greater trochanter of the hip
options.rationale: Near miss concept The greater trochanter is a landmark for the ventrogluteal site.

options.text: 2 to 3 fingerbreadths below the acromion, above the armpit
options.rationale: The deltoid site is 2 to 3 fingerbreadths below the acromion and above the level of the armpit, in the center of an inverted triangle on the lateral arm.

options.text: Halfway between the elbow and the shoulder on the back
options.rationale: Near miss concept The back of the arm is a subcutaneous site.

questions.takeaway: Deltoid: below the acromion, above the armpit.
questions.strategy: Use the bony landmark.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the Z track technique?

options.text: To make the injection less painful by numbing the skin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Z track does not numb the skin.

options.text: To keep the medication in the muscle from leaking back
options.rationale: Pulling the skin aside before inserting the needle and releasing it after creates a zigzag track that seals the medication in the muscle so it cannot leak into the subcutaneous tissue.

options.text: To allow a larger volume to be given in the deltoid
options.rationale: Near miss concept It does not increase the safe volume.

options.text: To let the nurse avoid aspirating before injecting
options.rationale: Near miss concept It is not a substitute for any other step.

questions.takeaway: Z track seals the drug in the muscle.
questions.strategy: Think about where the drug could leak.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct steps for preparing medications from ampules and vials.

options.text: Inject air into a vial before withdrawing
options.rationale: A filter needle keeps glass from an ampule out of the syringe, then is replaced. Air injected into a vial prevents a vacuum. When mixing a vial and an ampule, draw from the vial first, then from the ampule with the same syringe and filter needle.

options.text: Use a filter needle to draw from an ampule
options.rationale: A filter needle keeps glass from an ampule out of the syringe, then is replaced. Air injected into a vial prevents a vacuum. When mixing a vial and an ampule, draw from the vial first, then from the ampule with the same syringe and filter needle.

options.text: Keep the same filter needle in place to inject the patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept The filter needle is replaced with the injection needle.

options.text: Shake a two chamber vial hard to mix it
options.rationale: Near miss concept Two chamber vials are rolled, not shaken.

options.text: Draw from the vial first when mixing a vial and an ampule
options.rationale: A filter needle keeps glass from an ampule out of the syringe, then is replaced. Air injected into a vial prevents a vacuum. When mixing a vial and an ampule, draw from the vial first, then from the ampule with the same syringe and filter needle.

options.text: Change the filter needle before injecting
options.rationale: A filter needle keeps glass from an ampule out of the syringe, then is replaced. Air injected into a vial prevents a vacuum. When mixing a vial and an ampule, draw from the vial first, then from the ampule with the same syringe and filter needle.

questions.takeaway: Ampule: filter needle, then change it. Vial: air in first.
questions.strategy: Each step prevents glass, vacuum or contamination.

questions.stem: What is the current practice for rotating insulin injection sites?

options.text: Use a different body area for every injection
options.rationale: Near miss concept Changing areas each time changes absorption speed.

options.text: Use the same exact spot each time
options.rationale: Near miss concept Using one spot causes tissue hypertrophy.

options.text: Rotate only when bruising appears
options.rationale: Correct but premature Rotation is routine, not a response to bruising.

options.text: Choose one anatomical area and rotate within it
options.rationale: Absorption differs by area, so one anatomical site is chosen and injections rotate within that region. This keeps absorption consistent and prevents tissue damage.

questions.takeaway: Insulin: rotate within one region.
questions.strategy: Consistency of absorption is the goal.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct practices for giving enoxaparin from a prefilled syringe.

options.text: Insert at 10 to 15 degrees with the bevel up
options.rationale: Near miss concept Intradermal technique.

options.rationale: Subcutaneous injections are given at 45 to 90 degrees depending on tissue depth, and aspiration is not performed. Massaging a heparin site increases bruising. The shallow bevel up technique belongs to intradermal injection.

options.text: Insert at 45 degrees and massage the site after withdrawal
options.rationale: Near miss concept Correct angle, and massage increases bruising with heparin.

options.text: Insert at 90 degrees and aspirate before injecting
options.rationale: Near miss concept A correct angle paired with an action that does not belong.

questions.stem: A nurse is giving an intramuscular injection of a medication that is irritating to subcutaneous tissue. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Pull skin aside, inject at 90 degrees, wait 10 seconds, then release
options.rationale: This is the Z track technique. Displacing the skin, injecting, pausing so the medication disperses, then releasing the tissue seals the drug in the muscle and keeps it out of the subcutaneous layer. The dorsogluteal site is no longer used because of the sciatic nerve and the superior gluteal artery; the ventrogluteal site is preferred.

options.text: Inject at 90 degrees into the dorsogluteal site, then massage the site
options.rationale: Near miss concept An abandoned site, plus massage, which defeats the seal.

options.text: Pinch the tissue, inject at 90 degrees, and withdraw right away
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pinching is subcutaneous technique and the pause is missing.

options.text: Inject at 45 degrees into the ventrogluteal site with firm pressure after
options.rationale: Near miss concept Correct site, and 45 degrees is subcutaneous.

questions.takeaway: Z track for irritating drugs, and the ventrogluteal site for intramuscular injections.
questions.strategy: Two options here fail on the site rather than the technique. Check both.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct injection practices.

A shared multi dose vial has caused real hepatitis outbreaks, and the mechanism was the reused syringe rather than the needle: a new needle on an old syringe still carries blood back into the vial. A vial used for more than one patient is accessed only in the clean medication area with a new needle and a new syringe, and any vial that goes into a patient's room belongs to that patient alone.

questions.stem: Match each description to the injection route.

rows.text: 90 degrees into the ventrogluteal site, up to about 3 mL in an adult
45 to 90 degrees, no aspiration, pinch if tissue is thin
Z track technique for a medication that irritates tissue
10 to 15 degrees, bevel up, a wheal is expected

questions.takeaway: The angle tells you the depth and the depth tells you the route. Intradermal is almost flat and leaves a visible wheal, which is how a tuberculin test is read. Subcutaneous is 45 to 90 and is never aspirated. Intramuscular is 90 into the ventrogluteal site, and Z track seals an irritating drug inside the muscle. Do not aspirate a subcutaneous injection. That reflex is borrowed from intramuscular technique.
questions.strategy: Check the angle against the route, then check whether aspiration or a wheal belongs to that route at all.

questions.stem: Seventy two hours after a tuberculin skin test, a raised, hard area of induration has formed at the site. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Apply a warm compress and recheck tomorrow
options.rationale: Correct but premature The result needs reporting now.

options.text: Massage the area to reduce the swelling
options.rationale: Near miss concept Massage does not change the result and irritates the site.

options.text: Notify the provider and document the result
options.rationale: Induration at an intradermal test site may be a positive result. The nurse notifies the provider and documents the sensitivity or positive test.

options.text: Repeat the test on the other arm
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Repeating the test is not the nurse's decision.

questions.takeaway: Induration: report and document.

questions.stem: While giving an intramuscular injection, the nurse pulls back on the plunger and sees blood in the syringe. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Inject slowly, since a little blood is expected
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blood means the needle may be in a vessel.

options.text: Stop, remove the needle and prepare a new dose
options.rationale: Blood on aspiration means the needle may be in a blood vessel. The nurse stops, removes the needle, discards the syringe and prepares a new dose.

options.text: Move the needle slightly deeper and then inject the dose
options.rationale: Near miss concept The syringe is now contaminated with blood.

options.text: Inject the medication and apply pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Injecting may deliver the drug into a vessel.

questions.takeaway: Blood in the syringe: stop, discard, start over.

questions.stem: After a subcutaneous injection, a patient reports numbness, tingling and burning at the site that does not go away. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Massage the site to spread the medication
options.rationale: Near miss concept Massage can worsen tissue injury.

options.text: Assess the site, notify the provider and do not reuse it
options.rationale: Persistent pain, numbness, tingling or burning may mean nerve or tissue injury. The nurse assesses the site, notifies the provider and avoids that site.

options.rationale: Correct but premature Possible nerve injury needs reporting now.

options.text: Reassure the patient that this is expected
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Persistent numbness and burning are not expected.

questions.stem: A patient who injects insulin into the same area of the abdomen has a firm, thickened patch of skin there. What should the nurse teach?

options.text: Massage the thickened area before each injection
options.rationale: Near miss concept Massage does not resolve hypertrophy.

options.text: Switch to intramuscular insulin injections
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Insulin is not given intramuscularly for routine use.

options.text: Keep injecting into the thickened area, since it is less painful there
options.rationale: Near miss concept Absorption from hypertrophied tissue is unreliable.

options.text: Avoid that area for 6 months and rotate within another region
options.rationale: Repeated injections into one spot cause tissue hypertrophy and unreliable absorption. The patient avoids that area for 6 months and rotates within another region.

questions.takeaway: Hypertrophy: avoid the area for 6 months.
questions.strategy: Fix the cause, which is not rotating.

questions.stem: A nurse draws up a dose and notices the syringe contains more medication than ordered. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Discard the dose and prepare a correct new one
options.rationale: If an incorrect dose is prepared, the nurse discards it and prepares a new, correct dose. Air bubbles are expelled and the dose adjusted before injecting.

options.text: Squirt the extra back into the vial
options.rationale: Near miss concept Returning drug to a vial contaminates it.

options.text: Give it and document the difference in the medication record
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Documenting an error does not prevent it.

options.text: Give it, since the extra is small
options.rationale: Near miss concept Any extra is a dosing error.

questions.takeaway: Wrong dose drawn up: discard and redo.
questions.strategy: Do not return drug to a stock vial.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetes becomes confused and diaphoretic an hour after lunch. What should the nurse do first?

Master gland that directs other glands

options.rationale: ADH controls water balance. Too little causes diabetes insipidus: large volumes of dilute urine and thirst. The nurse watches urine output, fluid balance and sodium.

options.text: Serum sodium
options.rationale: ADH controls water balance. Too little causes diabetes insipidus: large volumes of dilute urine and thirst. The nurse watches urine output, fluid balance and sodium.

options.text: Visual acuity of the left eye only
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data This is not a priority link to ADH.

questions.takeaway: ADH problem: watch urine and sodium.
questions.strategy: Follow the hormone to water and sodium.

questions.stem: Classify each finding as hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism.

rows.text: Weight loss despite a good appetite

questions.takeaway: Too much thyroid hormone speeds metabolism: heat intolerance, sweating, weight loss, tremor, fast heart rate. Too little slows it: cold intolerance, weight gain, fatigue, constipation, slow heart rate and reflexes. Hyper speeds up, hypo slows down.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the body is running fast or slow.

questions.stem: Which finding suggests hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism?

options.text: Muscle weakness with confusion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Weakness and confusion go with high calcium.

options.text: Polyuria and thirst
options.rationale: Near miss concept Polyuria and thirst suggest hyperglycemia.

options.text: Kidney stones
options.rationale: Near miss concept Kidney stones go with high calcium.

options.text: A positive Chvostek sign
options.rationale: Low calcium makes nerves and muscles irritable: tetany, a positive Chvostek or Trousseau sign, seizures and dysrhythmias. Seizure and fall precautions apply.

questions.takeaway: Low calcium = twitchy.
questions.strategy: Low calcium excites; high calcium sedates.

questions.stem: Which adrenal hormone holds sodium and water to maintain blood pressure?

options.text: Cortisol
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cortisol affects glucose, immunity and inflammation.

options.text: Epinephrine
options.rationale: Near miss concept Epinephrine is the fight or flight hormone.

options.text: Aldosterone
options.rationale: Aldosterone makes the kidneys keep sodium and water, which supports blood pressure. Adrenal problems can cause unstable pressure and sodium and potassium imbalances.

options.text: Glucagon
options.rationale: Near miss concept Glucagon comes from the pancreas.

questions.takeaway: Aldosterone: salt and water.
questions.strategy: Match the hormone to fluid balance.

questions.stem: Match each statement to insulin or glucagon.

rows.text: Signals the liver to release stored glucose

questions.takeaway: Insulin lowers glucose by moving it into cells and promoting storage, and is released after meals. Glucagon raises glucose by signaling the liver to release stored glucose, and is released when fasting. Insulin in, glucagon out.
questions.strategy: Ask which way glucose moves.

questions.stem: Classify each feature as type 1 or type 2 diabetes.
questions.takeaway: Type 1 is autoimmune destruction of beta cells with little or no insulin, so insulin is always required and DKA risk is high. Type 2 is insulin resistance with gradual onset, managed with lifestyle and medications, and may need insulin over time. Type 1: no insulin. Type 2: resistant insulin.
questions.strategy: Ask whether insulin is missing or ignored.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about the classic signs of diabetes.
questions.sentence: Frequent urination is [[1]], increased thirst is [[2]], and increased hunger is [[3]].

options.text: polydipsia
polyphagia
polyuria
polydipsia
polyuria
polyphagia
polyuria
polyphagia
polydipsia

questions.takeaway: The 3 Ps: polyuria (urine), polydipsia (thirst) and polyphagia (hunger). Other signs include fatigue, blurred vision, weight change, slow healing and frequent infections. Uria urine, dipsia drink, phagia eat.
questions.strategy: Use the word roots.

questions.stem: Why does hyperglycemia cause frequent urination?

options.text: Glucose in the urine pulls water with it
options.rationale: When glucose spills into the urine it draws water by osmosis (osmotic diuresis). The result is polyuria, dehydration and electrolyte loss, so the nurse monitors hydration, intake and output and labs.

options.text: High glucose damages the bladder wall
options.rationale: Near miss concept The bladder is not the cause.

options.text: Insulin causes the kidneys to make more urine
options.rationale: Near miss concept Insulin does not cause polyuria.

options.text: Thirst causes the patient to drink more
options.rationale: Near miss concept Thirst follows the fluid loss; it is not the cause.

questions.takeaway: Sugar pulls water.
questions.strategy: Find the first step in the chain.

questions.stem: Classify each feature as DKA or HHS.

rows.text: Profound dehydration with prominent altered mental status

questions.takeaway: DKA comes from severe insulin deficiency: fat breaks down into ketones, causing metabolic acidosis over hours, mostly in type 1. HHS is extreme hyperglycemia and dehydration without significant ketones, developing over days, mostly in type 2. Both are emergencies. DKA ketones and fast. HHS dry and slow.
questions.strategy: Ketones decide it.

questions.stem: Select all of the common causes of hypoglycemia.

options.text: Alcohol without food
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia comes from too much medication or too little fuel: excess insulin, missed meals, too little carbohydrate, extra activity or alcohol without food.

options.text: Exercise without adjusting food or medication
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia comes from too much medication or too little fuel: excess insulin, missed meals, too little carbohydrate, extra activity or alcohol without food.

options.text: An infection causing stress
options.rationale: Near miss concept Illness and stress usually raise glucose.

options.text: A missed or delayed meal
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia comes from too much medication or too little fuel: excess insulin, missed meals, too little carbohydrate, extra activity or alcohol without food.

options.text: Too much insulin
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia comes from too much medication or too little fuel: excess insulin, missed meals, too little carbohydrate, extra activity or alcohol without food.

options.text: Skipping a dose of insulin
options.rationale: Near miss concept A missed insulin dose raises glucose.

questions.takeaway: Too much drug or too little food.
questions.strategy: Ask which way each factor pushes glucose.

questions.stem: Select all of the foot care teaching points for a patient with diabetes.

options.text: Inspect the feet daily for wounds, redness or swelling
options.rationale: Neuropathy hides injuries, and poor circulation slows healing. Daily inspection, protective footwear, prompt reporting and follow up prevent ulcers and infection.

options.text: Go barefoot at home to let the feet breathe
options.rationale: Near miss concept Going barefoot exposes numb feet to injury.

options.text: Soak the feet in hot water each night
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reduced sensation can lead to burns; prolonged soaking softens skin.

options.text: Attend regular follow up appointments
options.rationale: Neuropathy hides injuries, and poor circulation slows healing. Daily inspection, protective footwear, prompt reporting and follow up prevent ulcers and infection.

options.text: Report any sore or cut promptly
options.rationale: Neuropathy hides injuries, and poor circulation slows healing. Daily inspection, protective footwear, prompt reporting and follow up prevent ulcers and infection.

options.text: Wear proper footwear at all times
options.rationale: Neuropathy hides injuries, and poor circulation slows healing. Daily inspection, protective footwear, prompt reporting and follow up prevent ulcers and infection.

questions.takeaway: Look daily, never barefoot, report early.
questions.strategy: The patient may not feel the injury.

questions.stem: Select all of the long term complications of diabetes.

options.text: Peripheral neuropathy
options.rationale: Persistent hyperglycemia damages vessels and nerves: eyes (retinopathy), kidneys (nephropathy), nerves (neuropathy), heart and vessels (MI, stroke) and skin and feet (poor healing, ulcers).

options.text: Hyperthyroidism
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diabetes does not cause hyperthyroidism.

options.text: Increased risk of heart attack and stroke
options.rationale: Persistent hyperglycemia damages vessels and nerves: eyes (retinopathy), kidneys (nephropathy), nerves (neuropathy), heart and vessels (MI, stroke) and skin and feet (poor healing, ulcers).

options.text: Nephropathy
options.rationale: Persistent hyperglycemia damages vessels and nerves: eyes (retinopathy), kidneys (nephropathy), nerves (neuropathy), heart and vessels (MI, stroke) and skin and feet (poor healing, ulcers).

options.text: Retinopathy
options.rationale: Persistent hyperglycemia damages vessels and nerves: eyes (retinopathy), kidneys (nephropathy), nerves (neuropathy), heart and vessels (MI, stroke) and skin and feet (poor healing, ulcers).

options.text: Improved wound healing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Wound healing is impaired, not improved.

questions.takeaway: Eyes, kidneys, nerves, heart, feet.
questions.strategy: Think of every organ that depends on small vessels.

questions.stem: A patient with hyperthyroidism reports feeling tired. An hour later, the heart rate has risen from 104 to 138 and the temperature from 37.4 to 39.2 °C. Which finding is the priority?

options.text: The patient's report of feeling warm
options.rationale: Near miss concept Feeling warm is expected; the measured rise is the concern.

options.text: The fatigue
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fatigue is common and not life threatening.

options.text: The rising heart rate and temperature
options.rationale: A rapidly rising heart rate and temperature in hyperthyroidism can signal thyroid storm, a life threatening emergency. The nurse monitors cardiovascular status and temperature closely and reports at once.

options.text: The patient's recent weight loss
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Weight loss is expected and chronic.

questions.takeaway: Hyperthyroid with rising HR and temp: think thyroid storm.
questions.strategy: Pick the unstable, worsening finding.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes is found unresponsive. The glucose is 38 mg/dL. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Correct but premature The patient needs treatment now.

options.text: Hold the next insulin dose and observe
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Holding insulin does not treat the current low.

options.text: Give orange juice by mouth
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing by mouth to an unresponsive patient; aspiration risk.

options.text: Give IV dextrose or glucagon per protocol
options.rationale: An unresponsive patient cannot swallow safely. Hypoglycemia is treated with IV dextrose or glucagon per protocol, then rechecked.

questions.takeaway: Cannot swallow: IV dextrose or glucagon.
questions.strategy: Check whether the mouth is safe.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes has a glucose of 486 mg/dL, deep rapid respirations, a fruity odor on the breath and is drowsy. What is the nurse's first priority?

options.text: Assess airway, breathing and circulation
options.rationale: Kussmaul respirations, fruity breath and very high glucose suggest DKA. The nurse assesses the ABCs, monitors vital signs, mental status and labs, and gives IV fluids and insulin per protocol.

options.text: Give the usual dose of long acting insulin
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Treatment follows the DKA protocol, not the routine dose.

options.text: Encourage the patient to drink juice
options.rationale: Near miss concept Juice raises glucose further.

options.text: Teach sick day rules
options.rationale: Correct but premature Teaching comes after the patient is stable.

questions.takeaway: DKA: ABCs, then fluids and insulin per protocol.
questions.strategy: Life threats before teaching.

questions.stem: An 81 year old with type 2 diabetes has had increasing confusion over 3 days. Glucose is 920 mg/dL, mucous membranes are dry, and urine ketones are negative. What does this suggest?

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.rationale: Gradual onset, extreme glucose, profound dehydration, altered mental status and no ketones point to HHS, an emergency more common in type 2.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept The glucose is very high.

options.text: Expected aging changes
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Confusion and a glucose of 920 are not expected.

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.rationale: Near miss concept DKA has ketones and develops over hours.

questions.takeaway: No ketones, very high glucose, confused: HHS.
questions.strategy: Ketones separate DKA from HHS.

questions.stem: A patient with low calcium reports tingling around the mouth. Tapping the cheek causes the facial muscles to twitch. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Report the finding and start seizure precautions
options.rationale: Perioral tingling and a positive Chvostek sign mean neuromuscular irritability from low calcium, which can progress to tetany, seizures and dysrhythmias. The nurse reports it, monitors the rhythm and uses seizure precautions.

options.text: Encourage the patient to rest in a dark room
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Rest does not address the risk.

options.text: Give the scheduled calcium dose early without an order
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing the dose timing needs an order.

options.text: Document a normal reflex
options.rationale: Near miss concept A positive Chvostek sign is not normal.

questions.takeaway: Positive Chvostek: report and protect.
questions.strategy: Anticipate where low calcium leads.

questions.stem: Place the links of the chain of infection in order.

options.text: Portal of entry
Infectious agent
Mode of transmission
Susceptible host
Reservoir
Portal of exit

questions.takeaway: An organism (agent) lives in a reservoir, leaves through a portal of exit, travels by a mode of transmission, enters through a portal of entry and infects a susceptible host. Breaking any link stops the infection. Agent, reservoir, exit, transmission, entry, host.
questions.strategy: Follow the organism from where it lives to the next person.

questions.stem: A nurse performs hand hygiene before touching a patient. Which link of the chain of infection does this break most directly?

options.text: The infectious agent itself
options.rationale: Near miss concept The organism still exists; it simply does not travel.

options.text: Reservoir
options.rationale: Near miss concept The reservoir is where the organism lives.

options.text: Mode of transmission
options.rationale: Hands carry organisms between patients. Hand hygiene breaks the mode of transmission.

options.text: Susceptible host
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hand hygiene does not change the patient's resistance.

questions.takeaway: Hands are the vehicle.
questions.strategy: Ask what the action stops from moving.

questions.stem: Match each situation to the correct hand hygiene method.

rows.text: Leaving the room of a patient with C. difficile
After removing gloves with no visible soil
Before entering a room for routine care
Caring for a patient with norovirus

questions.takeaway: Alcohol rub is preferred for most care because it is faster and less irritating. Soap and water is used when hands are visibly soiled and for C. difficile and norovirus, because alcohol does not kill spores. Spores and visible soil: soap and water.
questions.strategy: Ask whether alcohol can kill what is on the hands.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about hand hygiene.
questions.sentence: Hand hygiene uses at least [[1]] of friction over all surfaces, including the nails and between the fingers. It is [[2]] for reducing health care associated infections.

options.text: 5 seconds
10 seconds
20 seconds
the single most effective intervention
a minor supporting measure
needed only with gloves

questions.takeaway: At least 20 seconds of friction reaches all surfaces. Hand hygiene is the single most effective intervention for reducing health care associated infections. 20 seconds, every surface.
questions.strategy: Each blank stands alone.

questions.stem: Match each condition to the transmission based precaution.
questions.takeaway: Contact: MRSA, VRE, C. difficile. Droplet: influenza, pertussis, meningitis. Airborne: tuberculosis, measles, varicella. Airborne: TB, measles, chickenpox.
questions.strategy: Learn the airborne three; most others are droplet or contact.

questions.stem: Match each precaution to its required protection.
columns: N95 and a negative pressure room

rows.answer: N95 and a negative pressure room

questions.takeaway: Contact needs a gown and gloves at minimum. Droplet needs a surgical mask within 3 feet, plus gown and gloves if contact with secretions is expected. Airborne needs an N95 or higher respirator and a negative pressure room if available. Contact gown, droplet mask, airborne N95.
questions.strategy: Match the protection to the particle size.

questions.stem: Which patients are cared for using standard precautions?

options.text: All patients, regardless of diagnosis
options.rationale: Standard precautions apply to every patient because any patient may carry an organism. They include hand hygiene, PPE based on anticipated exposure, safe injections and cough etiquette.

options.text: Only patients with open wounds
options.rationale: Near miss concept Standard precautions are not limited to wounds.

options.text: Only patients in isolation rooms
options.rationale: Near miss concept Isolation adds transmission based precautions on top.

options.text: Only patients with a known infection
options.rationale: Near miss concept Many infections are not yet known.

questions.takeaway: Standard = everyone.
questions.strategy: Watch for options that limit who is protected.

questions.stem: Place the steps for putting on PPE in order.

options.text: Gloves over the gown cuffs
Gown
Hand hygiene
Goggles or face shield
Mask or respirator

questions.takeaway: Hand hygiene first, then the gown, then the mask or respirator (with a seal check for an N95), then eye protection, and gloves last so they cover the gown cuffs. Hands, gown, mask, goggles, gloves.
questions.strategy: Gloves go on last so they cover the gown.

questions.stem: When removing PPE, which item is removed first, and which is removed last?

options.text: Mask or respirator first, gloves last
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gloves are the most contaminated and come off first.

options.text: Gloves first, mask or respirator last
options.rationale: Gloves are most contaminated, so they come off first. The mask or respirator comes off last by the ties, without touching the front. A respirator is removed after leaving the room and closing the door. Hand hygiene follows removal of all PPE.

options.text: Gown first, goggles or face shield last
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gloves come off before the gown.

options.text: Goggles first, gown last
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gloves come off before the goggles.

questions.takeaway: Gloves first, mask last, hands after.
questions.strategy: Remove the dirtiest item first.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct techniques for removing PPE.

options.text: Use the glove in glove method
options.rationale: Glove in glove keeps skin off the outside of the gloves. The gown is pulled away touching only the inside. Goggles and masks are handled by the ties or bands. Hand hygiene is done after all PPE is off, and between steps if hands become contaminated.

options.text: Remove an N95 inside the patient's room
options.rationale: Near miss concept A respirator is removed after leaving the room.

options.text: Touch only the inside of the gown and roll it inside out
options.rationale: Glove in glove keeps skin off the outside of the gloves. The gown is pulled away touching only the inside. Goggles and masks are handled by the ties or bands. Hand hygiene is done after all PPE is off, and between steps if hands become contaminated.

options.text: Pull the mask off by the front
options.rationale: Near miss concept The front of the mask is contaminated.

options.text: Remove goggles by the headband or earpieces
options.rationale: Glove in glove keeps skin off the outside of the gloves. The gown is pulled away touching only the inside. Goggles and masks are handled by the ties or bands. Hand hygiene is done after all PPE is off, and between steps if hands become contaminated.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene after removing all PPE
options.rationale: Glove in glove keeps skin off the outside of the gloves. The gown is pulled away touching only the inside. Goggles and masks are handled by the ties or bands. Hand hygiene is done after all PPE is off, and between steps if hands become contaminated.

questions.takeaway: Touch clean parts only.
questions.strategy: The fronts and outsides are contaminated.

questions.stem: Classify each practice as medical or surgical asepsis.

rows.text: Sterile dressing change on a surgical wound
Hand hygiene before a meal tray

questions.takeaway: Medical asepsis (clean technique) reduces the number and spread of organisms. Surgical asepsis (sterile technique) eliminates all organisms and is used for invasive procedures. Clean reduces; sterile eliminates.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the body is being entered.

questions.stem: Select all of the principles of a sterile field.

options.text: A wet area of the field is contaminated
options.rationale: Only sterile touches sterile. The 1 inch border is contaminated, moisture wicks organisms through, the field must always be in view and above the waist, and nothing reaches, talks or coughs over it.

options.text: Talking over the field does not matter
options.rationale: Near miss concept Talking or coughing over the field contaminates it.

options.text: Never turn your back on the field
options.rationale: Only sterile touches sterile. The 1 inch border is contaminated, moisture wicks organisms through, the field must always be in view and above the waist, and nothing reaches, talks or coughs over it.

options.text: Items below the waist remain sterile
options.rationale: Near miss concept Anything below the waist is considered contaminated.

options.text: The 1 inch border is considered contaminated
options.rationale: Only sterile touches sterile. The 1 inch border is contaminated, moisture wicks organisms through, the field must always be in view and above the waist, and nothing reaches, talks or coughs over it.

options.text: Reaching over the field is acceptable if quick
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reaching over the field drops organisms onto it.

questions.takeaway: Border, moisture, back, waist, reach.
questions.strategy: If in doubt, it is contaminated.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures that follow standard precautions during nursing skills.

options.text: Keep the work surface clean and dry
options.rationale: Use gloves for body fluids, mucous membranes or nonintact skin; add a gown, mask and eye protection for splashes; clean shared equipment; keep surfaces clean and dry; and teach cough etiquette.

options.text: Reuse the same gloves between two patients
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gloves are changed between patients, with hand hygiene.

options.text: Ask coughing patients to use a tissue and discard it
options.rationale: Use gloves for body fluids, mucous membranes or nonintact skin; add a gown, mask and eye protection for splashes; clean shared equipment; keep surfaces clean and dry; and teach cough etiquette.

options.text: Gown, mask and eye protection when splashing is possible
options.rationale: Use gloves for body fluids, mucous membranes or nonintact skin; add a gown, mask and eye protection for splashes; clean shared equipment; keep surfaces clean and dry; and teach cough etiquette.

options.text: Clean gloves when contact with body fluids is expected
options.rationale: Use gloves for body fluids, mucous membranes or nonintact skin; add a gown, mask and eye protection for splashes; clean shared equipment; keep surfaces clean and dry; and teach cough etiquette.

options.text: Clean shared equipment between patients
options.rationale: Use gloves for body fluids, mucous membranes or nonintact skin; add a gown, mask and eye protection for splashes; clean shared equipment; keep surfaces clean and dry; and teach cough etiquette.

questions.takeaway: Protection matches the exposure.
questions.strategy: Reject anything that carries organisms between patients.

questions.stem: Select all of the factors that increase a patient's risk of infection.

options.text: An invasive device such as a catheter
options.rationale: Age, poor nutrition, stress and disease weaken defenses. Invasive procedures and devices open a portal of entry. These make the host susceptible.

options.text: Advanced age
options.rationale: Age, poor nutrition, stress and disease weaken defenses. Invasive procedures and devices open a portal of entry. These make the host susceptible.

options.text: Adequate protein intake
options.rationale: Near miss concept Good nutrition supports immunity.

options.text: Regular hand hygiene by staff
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hand hygiene lowers risk.

options.text: Chronic stress
options.rationale: Age, poor nutrition, stress and disease weaken defenses. Invasive procedures and devices open a portal of entry. These make the host susceptible.

options.text: Poor nutrition
options.rationale: Age, poor nutrition, stress and disease weaken defenses. Invasive procedures and devices open a portal of entry. These make the host susceptible.

questions.takeaway: Weak host or open portal.

questions.stem: A patient is admitted with fever, night sweats, weight loss and a cough lasting 4 weeks. Tuberculosis is suspected. Which room and PPE are needed?

options.text: Any room, since the diagnosis is not confirmed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Precautions start when the disease is suspected.

options.text: A private room, gown and gloves
options.rationale: Near miss concept Contact precautions do not stop airborne spread.

options.text: A negative pressure room and an N95 respirator
options.rationale: Suspected tuberculosis needs airborne precautions immediately: a negative pressure room and an N95 or higher respirator.

options.text: A semiprivate room and a surgical mask
options.rationale: Near miss concept A surgical mask does not filter airborne particles.

questions.takeaway: Suspected TB: airborne now.
questions.strategy: Precautions follow suspicion, not confirmation.

questions.stem: A nurse is leaving the room of a patient with C. difficile diarrhea after removing gloves. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wash with soap and water
options.rationale: Soap and water with friction physically removes C. difficile spores, which alcohol cannot kill.

options.text: Skip hand hygiene, since gloves were worn
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gloves can tear and hands can be contaminated during removal.

options.text: Use hand rub, then put on new gloves
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hand rub still does not remove spores.

options.text: Use alcohol based hand rub at the doorway
options.rationale: Near miss concept Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores.

questions.takeaway: C. difficile: soap and water.
questions.strategy: Spores need mechanical removal.

questions.stem: During a sterile dressing change, a drop of saline soaks into the edge of the sterile drape where the gauze is resting. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Consider the field contaminated and set up a new one
options.rationale: Moisture contaminates a sterile field because it lets organisms wick through from below. The field and items on it are considered contaminated, and a new field is set up.

options.text: Move the gauze to a dry area of the drape
options.rationale: Near miss concept The gauze has already been exposed.

options.text: Blot the wet area with sterile gauze and continue
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blotting does not undo contamination.

options.text: Continue, since saline is sterile
options.rationale: Near miss concept Moisture wicks organisms through from the surface below.

questions.takeaway: Wet field = contaminated field.
questions.strategy: When in doubt, start over.

questions.stem: While removing a gown, a nurse's bare hand touches the outside front of the gown. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wipe the hand on the inside of the gown
options.rationale: Near miss concept Wiping does not remove organisms.

options.text: Finish removing all PPE, then perform hand hygiene once
options.rationale: Correct but premature Contaminated hands would spread organisms to the remaining PPE and face.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene now, then continue removing PPE
options.rationale: If hands become contaminated during removal, the nurse performs hand hygiene before continuing, then again after all PPE is off.

options.text: Put on a clean gown and start over
options.rationale: Near miss concept Putting on more PPE does not clean the hand.

questions.takeaway: Contaminated hands mid removal: clean them now.
questions.strategy: Protect the face and remaining PPE.

questions.stem: A patient has influenza. The nurse needs to give oral medications. What PPE is required at minimum?

options.text: A gown and gloves only, with no mask
options.rationale: Near miss concept Contact PPE alone does not block droplets.

options.text: No PPE, since the visit is brief
options.rationale: Near miss concept Brief contact still allows droplet spread.

options.text: A surgical mask when within 3 feet of the patient
options.rationale: Influenza is spread by large respiratory droplets. Droplet precautions require a surgical mask within 3 feet, adding gown and gloves if contact with secretions is expected.

options.text: An N95 respirator and a negative pressure room for the patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept Influenza spreads by droplets, not airborne particles.

questions.takeaway: Influenza: droplet mask.
questions.strategy: Match the PPE to the route.

questions.stem: Classify each IV solution by tonicity.
questions.takeaway: Isotonic: 0.9% sodium chloride, lactated Ringer's and D5W in the bag. Hypertonic: 3% sodium chloride, D10W, D5NS and D5LR. Hypotonic: 0.45% and 0.225% sodium chloride. Half normal is hypo; 3% is hyper.
questions.strategy: Ask where the water will move and what the patient can tolerate.

questions.stem: Match each solution type to what happens to the cells.
questions.takeaway: Water moves toward the higher concentration. Hypertonic fluid pulls water out of cells into the vessels. Hypotonic fluid pushes water into cells. Isotonic fluid causes no net shift. Water follows solute.
questions.strategy: Ask where the water will move and what the patient can tolerate.

questions.stem: Which patient should not receive 0.45% sodium chloride?

options.text: A patient with hypertonic dehydration and a high serum sodium level
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hypertonic dehydration is an indication.

options.text: A patient with cellular dehydration
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cellular dehydration is an indication.

options.text: A patient with a head injury and rising intracranial pressure
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid moves water into cells, including brain cells, which worsens cerebral edema. It is avoided with high ICP, head trauma, hypotension and third spacing.

options.text: A patient with DKA after initial fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Near miss concept DKA maintenance after initial resuscitation is an indication.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic plus brain injury: no.
questions.strategy: Ask what swelling brain cells would do.

questions.stem: Why does D5W act as a hypotonic solution in the body even though it is isotonic in the bag?

options.text: The bag concentrates as it warms
options.rationale: Near miss concept Warming does not change tonicity.

options.text: It draws water out of the cells
options.rationale: Near miss concept That describes a hypertonic effect.

options.text: The dextrose is metabolized, leaving free water
options.rationale: Once the dextrose is used by cells, only free water remains, which moves into cells like a hypotonic fluid. It is used cautiously where cerebral edema is a risk.

options.text: The sodium in it is excreted quickly
options.rationale: Near miss concept D5W contains no sodium.

questions.takeaway: D5W becomes free water.
questions.strategy: Follow what happens to the dextrose.

questions.stem: Select all of the requirements before starting a blood transfusion.

options.text: Baseline temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure and SpO2
options.rationale: Consent comes first, then two nurse verification of the label, ABO and Rh type, unit number and expiration against the band. An 18 to 20 gauge line and 0.9% sodium chloride are used, and baseline vitals are recorded.

options.text: An 18 to 20 gauge IV
options.rationale: Consent comes first, then two nurse verification of the label, ABO and Rh type, unit number and expiration against the band. An 18 to 20 gauge line and 0.9% sodium chloride are used, and baseline vitals are recorded.

options.text: Hang it with D5W
options.rationale: Near miss concept Only 0.9% sodium chloride is used; dextrose can damage red cells.

options.text: Two licensed nurses verify the unit and the patient
options.rationale: Consent comes first, then two nurse verification of the label, ABO and Rh type, unit number and expiration against the band. An 18 to 20 gauge line and 0.9% sodium chloride are used, and baseline vitals are recorded.

options.text: Pick up the blood before consent is obtained
options.rationale: Near miss concept Consent must be on file before the unit leaves the blood bank.

options.text: Written informed consent on file
options.rationale: Consent comes first, then two nurse verification of the label, ABO and Rh type, unit number and expiration against the band. An 18 to 20 gauge line and 0.9% sodium chloride are used, and baseline vitals are recorded.

questions.takeaway: Consent, two nurses, 18 to 20 gauge, saline only, baseline vitals.
questions.strategy: Each step prevents a fatal mismatch or reaction.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about transfusion monitoring.
questions.sentence: After starting a unit of packed red blood cells, the nurse reassesses vital signs at [[1]], then every [[2]], and the unit must be finished within [[3]].

options.text: 1 hour
15 minutes
4 hours
5 minutes
2 hours
30 to 60 minutes
4 hours
8 hours
24 hours

questions.takeaway: Most serious reactions occur early, so vitals are rechecked at 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes and at completion. Each unit is transfused within 4 hours to limit bacterial growth. 15 minutes, then 30 to 60, done in 4 hours.

options.text: Initial vascular access assessment and site selection
options.rationale: The RN performs initial assessment, insertion, blood transfusions, high alert IV drugs, interpretation and teaching. Assistive personnel can take vital signs and report site appearance. The RN stays accountable for anything delegated.

options.text: Reporting how the IV site looks
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Assistive personnel can report what they see.

options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Assistive personnel can take vital signs.

options.text: Giving a high alert IV medication
options.rationale: The RN performs initial assessment, insertion, blood transfusions, high alert IV drugs, interpretation and teaching. Assistive personnel can take vital signs and report site appearance. The RN stays accountable for anything delegated.

options.text: Teaching the patient about the infusion
options.rationale: The RN performs initial assessment, insertion, blood transfusions, high alert IV drugs, interpretation and teaching. Assistive personnel can take vital signs and report site appearance. The RN stays accountable for anything delegated.

options.text: Starting a blood transfusion
options.rationale: The RN performs initial assessment, insertion, blood transfusions, high alert IV drugs, interpretation and teaching. Assistive personnel can take vital signs and report site appearance. The RN stays accountable for anything delegated.

questions.takeaway: Assess, start blood, high alert, teach: RN.
questions.strategy: Judgment and high risk tasks stay with the RN.
