questions.stem: Match each situation to the usual catheter gauge.

rows.text: Major trauma with rapid fluid resuscitation

questions.takeaway: Larger gauge numbers are smaller catheters. 14 to 16 is for trauma and rapid fluids, 18 is preferred for blood, 20 is standard for adults and 22 to 24 is for children, older adults and fragile veins. Bigger emergency, smaller gauge number.
questions.strategy: Match the flow needed to the lumen.

questions.stem: Select all of the sites the nurse avoids for a peripheral IV.

options.text: A site distal to a recent infiltration
options.rationale: Avoid the mastectomy side, a fistula arm, paralyzed limbs, sites distal to prior infiltration or phlebitis, the antecubital fossa for short IVs and the legs in adults. Choose the most distal appropriate site first.

options.text: A forearm vein that is soft and straight
options.rationale: Near miss concept A soft, straight, resilient forearm vein is preferred.

options.text: The arm on the side of a mastectomy
options.rationale: Avoid the mastectomy side, a fistula arm, paralyzed limbs, sites distal to prior infiltration or phlebitis, the antecubital fossa for short IVs and the legs in adults. Choose the most distal appropriate site first.

options.text: The lower extremities in an adult
options.rationale: Avoid the mastectomy side, a fistula arm, paralyzed limbs, sites distal to prior infiltration or phlebitis, the antecubital fossa for short IVs and the legs in adults. Choose the most distal appropriate site first.

options.text: A paralyzed extremity
options.rationale: Avoid the mastectomy side, a fistula arm, paralyzed limbs, sites distal to prior infiltration or phlebitis, the antecubital fossa for short IVs and the legs in adults. Choose the most distal appropriate site first.

options.text: An arm with a dialysis fistula
options.rationale: Avoid the mastectomy side, a fistula arm, paralyzed limbs, sites distal to prior infiltration or phlebitis, the antecubital fossa for short IVs and the legs in adults. Choose the most distal appropriate site first.

questions.takeaway: Avoid damaged, protected or downstream sites.
questions.strategy: Ask whether fluid could back up or vessels are needed for something else.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct steps for chlorhexidine skin prep before inserting an IV.

options.text: Use chlorhexidine for patients older than 2 months
options.rationale: Chlorhexidine is scrubbed back and forth for at least 30 seconds and left to air dry completely. The site is not blotted, fanned or touched again.

options.text: Blot the site dry with gauze
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blotting removes the antiseptic before it works.

options.text: Let it air dry completely
options.rationale: Chlorhexidine is scrubbed back and forth for at least 30 seconds and left to air dry completely. The site is not blotted, fanned or touched again.

options.text: Scrub back and forth with friction for at least 30 seconds
options.rationale: Chlorhexidine is scrubbed back and forth for at least 30 seconds and left to air dry completely. The site is not blotted, fanned or touched again.

options.text: Repalpate the vein after cleaning to confirm it
options.rationale: Near miss concept Repalpating recontaminates the cleaned site.

options.text: Fan the site to speed drying
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fanning recontaminates and does not allow full drying.

questions.takeaway: Scrub 30 seconds, air dry, do not touch.
questions.strategy: Anything that touches the site after cleaning contaminates it.

questions.stem: Classify each device as peripheral or central access.
questions.takeaway: The location of the catheter tip, not the insertion site, defines central access. A PICC is central even though it is inserted in the arm. A midline ends below the axilla and is not a central line. Tip location decides.
questions.strategy: Ask where the tip ends.

questions.stem: What must happen before a newly placed PICC is used?

options.text: The transparent dressing must be changed once by the nurse
options.rationale: Near miss concept The dressing does not need changing before use.

options.text: The patient must sign a second consent
options.rationale: Near miss concept No second consent is required.

options.text: An x ray must confirm the tip placement
options.rationale: The PICC tip should sit in the lower superior vena cava. An x ray confirms placement before any infusion.

options.text: The line must be flushed with heparin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Flushing does not confirm placement.

questions.takeaway: PICC: x ray before use.
questions.strategy: Confirm the tip before using a central line.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct teaching points for a patient going home with a PICC.

options.text: Lift as much as needed with that arm
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heavy lifting over 10 lb with that arm is avoided.

options.text: Shower with a waterproof cover over the site
options.rationale: Keep the dressing clean, dry and intact, cover it to shower, avoid submerging, avoid pressure and needles on that arm, limit lifting, stop if there is resistance and report signs of infection, clot or breakage.

options.text: Do not flush if resistance is felt and call for help
options.rationale: Keep the dressing clean, dry and intact, cover it to shower, avoid submerging, avoid pressure and needles on that arm, limit lifting, stop if there is resistance and report signs of infection, clot or breakage.

options.text: No blood pressure cuffs or blood draws on the PICC arm
options.rationale: Keep the dressing clean, dry and intact, cover it to shower, avoid submerging, avoid pressure and needles on that arm, limit lifting, stop if there is resistance and report signs of infection, clot or breakage.

options.text: Swim to keep the arm active
options.rationale: Near miss concept Submerging the arm is avoided.

options.text: Report fever, redness, swelling or drainage
options.rationale: Keep the dressing clean, dry and intact, cover it to shower, avoid submerging, avoid pressure and needles on that arm, limit lifting, stop if there is resistance and report signs of infection, clot or breakage.

questions.takeaway: Dry, protected, no pressure, report changes.
questions.strategy: Protect the line and the arm.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures in the central line infection prevention bundle.

options.text: Choosing the femoral site whenever possible
options.rationale: Near miss concept The femoral site has the highest infection risk.

options.text: Daily review of whether the line is still needed
options.rationale: Hand hygiene, maximal barriers, chlorhexidine prep, site selection that favors the subclavian over the femoral site and a daily necessity review reduce central line bloodstream infections.

options.text: Hand hygiene before any access
options.rationale: Hand hygiene, maximal barriers, chlorhexidine prep, site selection that favors the subclavian over the femoral site and a daily necessity review reduce central line bloodstream infections.

options.text: Leaving the line in place in case it is needed later
options.rationale: Near miss concept Every extra day of dwell raises infection risk.

options.text: Maximal sterile barriers during insertion
options.rationale: Hand hygiene, maximal barriers, chlorhexidine prep, site selection that favors the subclavian over the femoral site and a daily necessity review reduce central line bloodstream infections.

options.text: Chlorhexidine skin prep allowed to dry
options.rationale: Hand hygiene, maximal barriers, chlorhexidine prep, site selection that favors the subclavian over the femoral site and a daily necessity review reduce central line bloodstream infections.

questions.takeaway: Hands, barriers, CHG, best site, remove when not needed.
questions.strategy: Each step removes an infection source.

questions.stem: Classify each finding as infiltration or phlebitis.

rows.text: A palpable cord along the vein
Slowed drip rate with no blood return
Warmth and pain along the vein

questions.takeaway: Infiltration is fluid leaking into tissue: cool, pale, swollen, slow flow. Phlebitis is inflammation of the vein: red, warm, painful, a streak or cord. Both require stopping the infusion and removing the catheter. Infiltration cool and pale; phlebitis red and hot.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the problem is fluid in tissue or an angry vein.

questions.stem: How is speed shock prevented?

options.text: Warming the IV fluid before hanging it
options.rationale: Near miss concept Warming does not control the rate.

options.text: Changing the tubing every 24 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tubing changes prevent infection, not speed shock.

options.text: Flushing the line with heparin first before every single infusion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heparin does not control the infusion rate.

options.text: Using a pump and verifying the rate before starting
options.rationale: Speed shock comes from a drug or fluid given too fast: flushing, headache, chest tightness and shock. Pumps, rate checks and never bolusing concentrated drugs prevent it.

questions.takeaway: Speed shock: pump and rate check.
questions.strategy: Match the prevention to the cause.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to give an intravenous push medication through an existing peripheral line. Which action is essential before administering it?

options.text: Assess the site for patency and signs of infiltration or phlebitis
options.rationale: An intravenous push delivers the full dose in seconds, so an infiltrated site puts a concentrated drug into tissue with no way to take it back. You check the site and patency first, then push at the rate the drug requires, which for most medications is measured in minutes rather than seconds.

options.text: Raise the infusion bag to increase flow before the push
options.rationale: Near miss concept Changes gravity flow and tells you nothing about the site.

options.text: Disconnect the primary tubing and administer directly into the catheter hub
options.rationale: Near miss concept Breaks a closed system unnecessarily.

options.text: Give the medication as fast as the line allows to ensure a therapeutic level
options.rationale: Near miss concept Push rates are drug specific and exceeding them causes harm.

questions.takeaway: The faster the delivery, the more the site assessment matters.
questions.strategy: Rate options in intravenous push items are usually the trap. Faster is not better.

questions.stem: A patient with a central line suddenly becomes short of breath with chest pain and hypotension after the tubing disconnects. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Remove the central line right away and apply firm pressure to the site
options.rationale: Near miss concept Removing the line can let in more air.

options.text: Start a rapid fluid bolus through the line
options.rationale: Near miss concept Infusing through an open line adds more air.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and give oxygen by cannula
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sitting up can let air travel to the brain; position matters.

options.text: Clamp the line and turn the patient to the left side, head down
options.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, chest pain and hypotension after a disconnection suggest an air embolism. Clamp the line, position the patient in left lateral Trendelenburg to trap air, call the rapid response team and give 100% oxygen.

questions.takeaway: Air embolism: clamp, left side head down.
questions.strategy: Stop the air, then trap it.

questions.stem: An IV site is red, warm and tender with a red streak and a palpable cord. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop the infusion, remove the catheter and apply a warm, moist compress
options.rationale: These are signs of phlebitis. The nurse stops the infusion, removes the catheter, applies a warm moist compress, notifies the provider and documents the grade.

options.text: Flush the line to clear any clot
options.rationale: Near miss concept Flushing can push a clot or irritant further.

options.text: Apply ice to the site and keep the infusion running at the same ordered rate
options.rationale: Near miss concept The infusion must be stopped.

options.text: Slow the infusion and recheck in an hour
options.rationale: Correct but premature The vein is already inflamed; slowing does not fix it.

questions.takeaway: Phlebitis: stop, remove, warm compress, report.
questions.strategy: Remove the cause.

questions.stem: Fifteen minutes into a transfusion, a patient develops chills, a temperature rise of 1.5 °C and low back pain. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the transfusion and keep the line open with saline on new tubing
options.rationale: Chills, fever and back pain early in a transfusion suggest a hemolytic reaction. The nurse stops the transfusion, keeps the vein open with 0.9% sodium chloride on new tubing, assesses and notifies the provider and blood bank.

options.text: Finish the unit quickly so the patient has less total exposure time to the blood
options.rationale: Near miss concept Giving more blood worsens a reaction.

options.text: Recheck the vital signs in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Correct but premature Waiting allows the reaction to progress.

options.text: Slow the transfusion and give acetaminophen
options.rationale: Correct but premature Slowing still delivers more incompatible blood.

questions.takeaway: Reaction: stop the blood, keep the vein open.
questions.strategy: Stop the exposure first.

questions.stem: An 86 year old with thin skin and fragile veins needs maintenance IV fluids. Which approach is best?

options.text: An 18 gauge catheter in a dorsal hand vein
options.rationale: Near miss concept A large catheter and dorsal hand veins raise infiltration and hematoma risk.

options.text: A 22 gauge catheter in the forearm with a gentle tourniquet
options.rationale: Older adults have fragile, rolling veins and thin skin. Use the smallest effective gauge (22 to 24), avoid overtightening the tourniquet, apply gentle traction and avoid dorsal hand veins when possible. Infuse at lower rates and watch for fluid overload.

options.text: A 16 gauge catheter in the antecubital fossa
options.rationale: Near miss concept The antecubital fossa is avoided for short IVs, and 16 gauge is too large.

options.text: A 20 gauge catheter in the lower leg, where the veins are often larger
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lower extremities are avoided in adults.

questions.takeaway: Older adult: small gauge, gentle technique, slower rate.
questions.strategy: Protect fragile veins and limited fluid tolerance.

questions.stem: A nurse notes that the skin around a peripheral intravenous site is cool, pale and swollen, and the infusion has slowed. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Elevate the extremity and continue the infusion at a reduced rate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Keeps fluid entering tissue that is already infiltrated.

options.text: Apply a warm compress to the site
options.rationale: Correct but premature A later step, and the wrong one for some agents.

options.text: Stop the infusion
options.rationale: Cool, pale, swollen tissue with a slowing infusion is infiltration. The first action is to stop the infusion so no more fluid enters the tissue. Elevation and a compress per policy follow, and the provider is notified if the agent was a vesicant or contained potassium.

options.text: Flush the catheter to confirm patency
options.rationale: Near miss concept Worsens the infiltration.

questions.takeaway: Stop first. Everything else is about limiting damage already done.
questions.strategy: Flushing a suspected infiltration pushes more fluid into the tissue.

questions.stem: Classify each situation as enteral or parenteral nutrition.

rows.text: Head and neck cancer with a functioning gut
Gut that cannot absorb adequate nutrients
Stroke with unsafe swallow and a working gut

questions.takeaway: If the gut works, use it: enteral nutrition delivers nutrients into the GI tract. Parenteral nutrition delivers them into a vein when the GI tract cannot be adequately used. If the gut works, use it.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the GI tract can be used.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings that suggest undernutrition.

options.text: Increased appetite
options.rationale: Near miss concept Poor appetite, not increased appetite, is a risk factor.

options.text: Weight gain from edema only
options.rationale: Near miss concept Edema can hide weight loss but is not a sign of good nutrition.

options.text: Poor wound healing
options.rationale: Undernutrition is intake or absorption that does not meet needs. Signs include unintentional weight loss, weakness, fatigue and poor wound healing. Identify deficits early and monitor the response to feeding.

options.text: Muscle weakness
options.rationale: Undernutrition is intake or absorption that does not meet needs. Signs include unintentional weight loss, weakness, fatigue and poor wound healing. Identify deficits early and monitor the response to feeding.

options.text: Unintentional weight loss
options.rationale: Undernutrition is intake or absorption that does not meet needs. Signs include unintentional weight loss, weakness, fatigue and poor wound healing. Identify deficits early and monitor the response to feeding.

options.text: Fatigue
options.rationale: Undernutrition is intake or absorption that does not meet needs. Signs include unintentional weight loss, weakness, fatigue and poor wound healing. Identify deficits early and monitor the response to feeding.

questions.takeaway: Loss, weakness, fatigue, poor healing.
questions.strategy: Pick signs of not enough fuel.

questions.stem: Match each feeding tube to its usual duration of use.
questions.takeaway: Nasal tubes are less invasive and used when feeding is brief. Gastrostomy and jejunostomy tubes are placed for prolonged support. Through the nose: short term. Through the abdomen: long term.
questions.strategy: Match the invasiveness to the duration.

questions.stem: Match each feature to the type of nasogastric tube.

rows.text: Used exclusively for feeding and medications
Used for gastric decompression and lavage

questions.takeaway: Large bore tubes such as the Salem sump are double lumen and used for decompression, lavage and medications. Small bore tubes such as the Dobhoff are single lumen and used only for feeding and medications. Large bore drains; small bore feeds.
questions.strategy: Match the size to the job.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct practices for confirming initial placement of a blindly inserted feeding tube.

options.text: Mark and document the external tube length
options.rationale: An x ray confirms a blindly inserted tube before formula, water or medications. The result is reviewed and the external length marked as a baseline for later checks.

options.text: Start the formula while waiting for the x ray
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing goes through the tube until placement is confirmed.

options.text: Obtain an x ray before using the tube
options.rationale: An x ray confirms a blindly inserted tube before formula, water or medications. The result is reviewed and the external length marked as a baseline for later checks.

options.text: Inject air and listen over the stomach
options.rationale: Near miss concept Air bolus auscultation does not reliably confirm placement.

options.text: Rely on the color of the aspirate alone
options.rationale: Near miss concept Aspirate appearance alone cannot guarantee placement.

options.text: Review the documented x ray result before use
options.rationale: An x ray confirms a blindly inserted tube before formula, water or medications. The result is reviewed and the external length marked as a baseline for later checks.

questions.takeaway: X ray first, mark the length.
questions.strategy: Reject methods that guess.

questions.stem: Select all of the ongoing checks for tube placement before a feeding.

options.text: Hold tube use and verify further if placement is uncertain
options.rationale: Before feedings and medications, compare external length with the baseline, check securement, use aspirate and pH per policy and stop if anything is uncertain.

options.text: Check aspirate and pH per policy
options.rationale: Before feedings and medications, compare external length with the baseline, check securement, use aspirate and pH per policy and stop if anything is uncertain.

options.text: Use an air bolus as the only check
options.rationale: Near miss concept Air bolus is not reliable.

options.text: Compare the external length with the documented baseline
options.rationale: Before feedings and medications, compare external length with the baseline, check securement, use aspirate and pH per policy and stop if anything is uncertain.

options.text: Assume placement is fine if the patient is not coughing
options.rationale: Near miss concept A displaced tube may cause no cough.

options.text: Check the securement and signs of displacement
options.rationale: Before feedings and medications, compare external length with the baseline, check securement, use aspirate and pH per policy and stop if anything is uncertain.

questions.takeaway: Length, securement, pH, stop if unsure.
questions.strategy: When in doubt, hold the tube.

questions.stem: Which statement about gastric aspirate pH is correct?

options.text: Acid suppressing drugs lower the gastric pH further
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acid suppressing drugs raise gastric pH.

options.text: Formula in the tube makes the pH more reliable
options.rationale: Near miss concept Formula makes pH less reliable.

options.text: Gastric aspirate is usually 5 or below, but pH alone cannot guarantee placement
options.rationale: Gastric aspirate is usually acidic, pH 5 or below. Acid suppressing drugs raise it, and formula makes it less reliable, so pH is interpreted with the whole assessment.

options.text: A pH of 7 always confirms the tube is in the stomach, so no other check is needed at all
options.rationale: Absolute language Always is wrong, and 7 is not typical of the stomach.

questions.takeaway: pH helps; it does not prove.
questions.strategy: Watch for always and for effects in the wrong direction.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about preventing aspiration during tube feeding.
questions.sentence: Keep the head of the bed at [[1]] during feeding. Feeding into the small intestine [[2]] aspiration risk.

options.text: 0 to 15 degrees
30 to 45 degrees
60 to 90 degrees
does not eliminate
completely eliminates
doubles

questions.takeaway: Head of bed 30 to 45 degrees during feeding reduces reflux into the airway. Small intestine feeding may lower the risk, but it does not eliminate it. 30 to 45 degrees; small bowel is not risk free.
questions.strategy: Look for absolute claims.

questions.stem: Match each description to the feeding method.

rows.text: Pump feeding over a set period such as overnight
A large volume given over a short time
Hourly rate through a pump around the clock

questions.takeaway: Bolus gives a larger volume quickly. Intermittent gives feedings at scheduled times. Continuous runs at an hourly rate on a pump. Cyclic runs on a pump over a set period, often overnight. Rates advance only as ordered. Bolus fast, intermittent scheduled, continuous constant, cyclic overnight.
questions.strategy: Focus on timing and volume.

questions.stem: Select all of the times the nurse flushes a feeding tube.

options.text: Never during continuous feeding
options.rationale: Near miss concept Continuous feedings need scheduled flushes.

options.text: At scheduled intervals during a continuous feeding
options.rationale: Flush with 30 mL of water (or as ordered) before and after intermittent feedings, at intervals during continuous feeding and before, between and after medications. Flushes count toward intake.

options.text: Before, between and after each medication
options.rationale: Flush with 30 mL of water (or as ordered) before and after intermittent feedings, at intervals during continuous feeding and before, between and after medications. Flushes count toward intake.

options.text: Before and after an intermittent feeding
options.rationale: Flush with 30 mL of water (or as ordered) before and after intermittent feedings, at intervals during continuous feeding and before, between and after medications. Flushes count toward intake.

options.text: Only when the tube is clogged
options.rationale: Correct but premature Flushing prevents clogs; waiting for one is too late.

options.text: Only at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Near miss concept Flushes are tied to feedings and medications, not shifts.

questions.takeaway: Flush around every feeding and every medication.
questions.strategy: Prevention, not rescue.

questions.stem: A small bore feeding tube is clogged. What should the nurse try first?

options.text: Gentle flushing with warm water
options.rationale: Gentle water flushing is tried first. Never force the tube, and avoid carbonated drinks and juice.

options.text: Forceful flushing with a 10 mL syringe
options.rationale: Near miss concept Force and small syringes can rupture the tube.

options.text: Instilling cola to dissolve the clog
options.rationale: Near miss concept Carbonated drinks are avoided; they can worsen clogs.

options.text: Instilling cranberry juice
options.rationale: Near miss concept Juice is avoided; acid can curdle formula.

questions.takeaway: Clog: gentle water, never force.
questions.strategy: Reject force and folk remedies.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings the nurse monitors for feeding tolerance.

options.text: Coughing, dyspnea or oxygen desaturation
options.rationale: Watch fullness, nausea, vomiting, pain and distention; stool pattern; formula actually delivered; intake and output, weight and labs; and respiratory signs of aspiration.

options.text: Stool frequency and consistency
options.rationale: Watch fullness, nausea, vomiting, pain and distention; stool pattern; formula actually delivered; intake and output, weight and labs; and respiratory signs of aspiration.

options.text: Formula delivered compared with the amount prescribed
options.rationale: Watch fullness, nausea, vomiting, pain and distention; stool pattern; formula actually delivered; intake and output, weight and labs; and respiratory signs of aspiration.

options.text: Changes in the color of the hair over the past several weeks
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Hair color is not a tolerance measure.

options.text: Eye color
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Eye color does not change with feeding.

options.text: Nausea, vomiting or abdominal distention
options.rationale: Watch fullness, nausea, vomiting, pain and distention; stool pattern; formula actually delivered; intake and output, weight and labs; and respiratory signs of aspiration.

questions.takeaway: Gut, stool, volume, breathing.
questions.strategy: Pick findings the feeding could change.

questions.stem: What is true about gastric residual volume?

options.text: It reliably predicts aspiration on its own
options.rationale: Near miss concept Residual volume alone does not reliably predict aspiration.

options.text: It is interpreted with vomiting, distention and other intolerance signs
options.rationale: Gastric residual volume is the amount withdrawn from the stomach. Facility policy decides whether and when to check, and it is read alongside vomiting, distention and other signs.

options.text: It must be checked every hour in every patient
options.rationale: Absolute language Checking follows facility policy, not a universal rule.

options.text: A high value always means the feeding should stop permanently
options.rationale: Absolute language Always and permanently overstate it.

questions.takeaway: Residual: one data point, read in context.
questions.strategy: Avoid options that make one number decisive.

questions.stem: What is refeeding syndrome?

options.text: Dangerous electrolyte shifts when restarting nutrition after severe undernutrition
options.rationale: In a severely undernourished patient, restarting nutrition drives potassium, magnesium and phosphate into cells, dropping blood levels dangerously. Monitor intake and output, daily weights and ordered labs.

options.text: An allergic reaction to a protein in the formula after the first feeding
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is an allergy.

options.text: A clogged tube from thick formula
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is a mechanical problem.

options.text: Diarrhea from formula given too cold
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is a feeding tolerance issue.

questions.takeaway: Refeeding: watch potassium, magnesium, phosphate.
questions.strategy: Link starvation, refeeding and electrolytes.

questions.stem: During a continuous tube feeding, a patient begins coughing, has noisy breathing and the SpO2 drops from 96% to 88%. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the feeding and assess airway and breathing
options.rationale: These are signs of aspiration. Stop the feeding, assess the airway and breathing, raise the head of the bed and get help.

options.text: Flush the tube with 30 mL of water
options.rationale: Near miss concept More fluid worsens aspiration.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed to rest the patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lowering the head increases aspiration.

options.text: Check the gastric residual volume
options.rationale: Correct but premature Residual checks can wait; the airway cannot.

questions.takeaway: Suspected aspiration: stop and assess the airway.
questions.strategy: Airway first.

questions.stem: Before an intermittent feeding, the nurse finds the external mark on the NG tube is 8 cm farther out than the documented length. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Retape the tube and start the feeding
options.rationale: Near miss concept Retaping does not confirm placement.

options.text: Push the tube back to the original mark and feed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Advancing blindly can send the tube into the airway.

options.text: Hold the feeding and verify placement
options.rationale: A change in external length suggests displacement. The nurse holds tube use and obtains further verification per policy.

options.text: Give the feeding slowly to test tolerance
options.rationale: Near miss concept Feeding a possibly displaced tube risks aspiration.

questions.takeaway: Length changed: hold and verify.
questions.strategy: Uncertain placement means nothing goes in.

questions.stem: A patient receiving tube feedings has had 5 liquid stools today. What should the nurse assess?

options.text: Nothing, since diarrhea is expected with tube feeding
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Diarrhea is not expected and needs a cause.

options.text: Only whether the formula rate is too slow
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rate alone is not the only cause.

options.text: Medications, infection, contamination and formula tolerance
options.rationale: Diarrhea during tube feeding can come from medications (such as antibiotics or sorbitol liquids), infection such as C. difficile, contaminated formula or intolerance.

options.text: Only whether the tube is in the jejunum
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tube position is one factor among many.

questions.takeaway: Diarrhea: drugs, bugs, contamination, tolerance.
questions.strategy: Look for every cause, not just one.

questions.stem: A bag of formula has been hanging longer than the facility's hang time limit, and half remains. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Refrigerate it and restart later
options.rationale: Near miss concept Opened formula past its hang time is not reused.

options.text: Continue until the bag is empty
options.rationale: Near miss concept Formula past its hang time can grow bacteria.

options.text: Discard it and hang fresh formula
options.rationale: Hang time limits prevent bacterial growth. Expired formula is discarded and fresh formula hung with labeled equipment, following manufacturer and facility limits.

options.text: Add fresh formula to the remaining amount
options.rationale: Near miss concept Mixing old and new spreads contamination.

questions.takeaway: Past hang time: discard.
questions.strategy: Contamination risk outweighs waste.

questions.stem: Match each device to its usual flow rate.
questions.takeaway: Nasal cannula 1 to 6 L/min, simple mask 5 to 10 L/min, nonrebreather 10 to 15 L/min and high flow nasal cannula up to about 60 L/min. 1 to 6, 5 to 10, 10 to 15, up to 60.
questions.strategy: Match the device to how much oxygen the patient needs.

questions.stem: Match each device to its approximate FiO2.
questions.takeaway: Nasal cannula delivers about 24 to 44%, simple mask about 40 to 60%, nonrebreather up to about 60 to 90% and high flow nasal cannula 21 to 100%, which can be set precisely. Cannula low, mask middle, nonrebreather high, high flow precise.
questions.strategy: Match the device to how much oxygen the patient needs.

questions.stem: Why is a simple face mask never run below 5 L/min?

options.text: The oxygen tank will run out faster
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lower flow uses less oxygen, not more.

options.text: The patient will not be able to speak
options.rationale: Near miss concept Flow does not affect speech.

options.text: The mask will not stay on the face
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fit does not depend on flow.

options.text: Exhaled carbon dioxide can be rebreathed
options.rationale: The flow flushes exhaled air out of the mask. Below 5 L/min, carbon dioxide builds up and is rebreathed.

questions.takeaway: Simple mask: 5 L/min minimum.
questions.strategy: Ask what clears the mask of exhaled air.

questions.stem: What must the nurse do before placing a nonrebreather mask on a patient?

options.text: Remove the one way valves
options.rationale: Near miss concept The valves keep exhaled air out of the bag.

options.text: Humidify the oxygen first
options.rationale: Near miss concept Humidification is not the required first step.

options.text: Inflate the reservoir bag
options.rationale: The reservoir bag holds high concentration oxygen for each breath. It is filled before the mask goes on and must stay partly inflated during inspiration.

options.text: Set the flow to 5 L/min
options.rationale: Near miss concept A nonrebreather runs at 10 to 15 L/min.

questions.takeaway: Fill the bag first.
questions.strategy: Without a full bag, the high concentration is lost.

questions.stem: Which statement about oxygen flow and FiO2 is correct?

options.text: FiO2 cannot change at all once the device has been applied to the patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept FiO2 varies with breathing pattern and fit.

options.text: Flow and FiO2 are always the same number
options.rationale: Absolute language Flow (L/min) and FiO2 (%) are different measures.

options.text: Delivered FiO2 depends on the patient's breathing and the device fit
options.rationale: Flow is how much oxygen leaves the wall. FiO2 is the fraction the patient actually inhales, which depends on breathing rate and depth, the airway and how well the device fits.

options.text: Raising flow always doubles the FiO2
options.rationale: Absolute language There is no fixed doubling.

questions.takeaway: Flow is not FiO2.
questions.strategy: Watch for always and never.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct nursing considerations for a nasal cannula.

options.text: Use it for patients who need a high concentration of oxygen
options.rationale: Near miss concept A cannula is for low levels of supplemental oxygen.

options.text: Place the prongs in the nares and loop the tubing over the ears
options.rationale: A nasal cannula is a low flow device. It allows eating and talking, but the tubing can cause pressure injuries on the ears and nares. If needs rise, a different device is anticipated.

options.text: The patient can eat, drink and talk
options.rationale: A nasal cannula is a low flow device. It allows eating and talking, but the tubing can cause pressure injuries on the ears and nares. If needs rise, a different device is anticipated.

options.text: Set the flow at 10 L/min for most patients
options.rationale: Near miss concept A nasal cannula runs at 1 to 6 L/min.

options.text: Assess the ears and nares for pressure injury
options.rationale: A nasal cannula is a low flow device. It allows eating and talking, but the tubing can cause pressure injuries on the ears and nares. If needs rise, a different device is anticipated.

options.text: Anticipate a different device if more oxygen is needed
options.rationale: A nasal cannula is a low flow device. It allows eating and talking, but the tubing can cause pressure injuries on the ears and nares. If needs rise, a different device is anticipated.

questions.takeaway: Cannula: low flow, check ears and nose.
questions.strategy: Know the limits of the device.

questions.stem: Match each feature to the device.

rows.text: Heated and humidified with a precisely set FiO2
Reservoir cannula that delivers a bolus on inhalation
Reservoir bag with one way valves for high concentration

questions.takeaway: An Oxymizer stores oxygen in a reservoir and releases a bolus on inhalation, making it more efficient than a cannula. High flow nasal cannula is heated and humidified with a precisely set FiO2. A nonrebreather uses a reservoir bag and valves for high concentration. Oxymizer conserves, high flow humidifies, nonrebreather concentrates.
questions.strategy: Match the key feature.

questions.stem: Place the steps for starting oxygen in order.

options.text: Apply the device and set the flow
Verify the order and select the device
Reassess SpO2 and work of breathing
Assess respiratory status and SpO2
Document the device, flow and response

questions.takeaway: Assess, verify, apply, reassess, document. Comparing the reassessment with the baseline shows whether the oxygen is working. Assess, apply, reassess.
questions.strategy: Bookend the intervention with assessment.

questions.stem: What does the nurse monitor specifically for a patient on high flow nasal cannula?

options.text: That the flow stays below 5 L/min
options.rationale: Near miss concept High flow runs up to about 60 L/min.

options.text: Whether the patient can blow out a candle
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is not a monitoring step.

options.text: Humidification and temperature of the gas
options.rationale: High flow nasal cannula delivers heated, humidified gas. The nurse monitors humidification and temperature along with SpO2, work of breathing and the skin of the nares and ears.

options.text: Whether the reservoir bag is inflated
options.rationale: Near miss concept There is no reservoir bag on high flow nasal cannula.

questions.takeaway: High flow: check the humidifier and heat.
questions.strategy: Monitor the feature that makes it different.

questions.stem: A patient on a nasal cannula at 6 L/min has an SpO2 of 86%, respirations of 30 and accessory muscle use. The order allows titration. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Increase the cannula to 10 L/min
options.rationale: Near miss concept A cannula above 6 L/min adds little and dries the mucosa.

options.text: Apply a nonrebreather at 10 to 15 L/min and notify the provider
options.rationale: The patient needs more oxygen than a cannula can provide. A nonrebreather gives a high concentration, and the provider is notified of the deterioration.

options.text: Change to a simple face mask at 4 L/min so the patient feels less closed in
options.rationale: Near miss concept A simple mask below 5 L/min causes rebreathing and gives less oxygen.

options.text: Recheck the SpO2 in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Correct but premature Waiting 30 minutes with this distress is unsafe.

questions.takeaway: Maxed cannula and still low: step up and notify.
questions.strategy: Match the device to the need.

questions.stem: A nurse finds a simple face mask running at 3 L/min on a patient. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Leave it as it is, since the SpO2 is 93% and the patient looks comfortable
options.rationale: Near miss concept Low flow lets carbon dioxide build up even if SpO2 looks acceptable.

options.text: Increase the flow to at least 5 L/min or change the device per order
options.rationale: A simple mask needs at least 5 L/min to flush exhaled carbon dioxide. The nurse corrects the flow or changes to an appropriate device per the order.

options.text: Turn the flow off to rest the patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept Turning it off removes prescribed oxygen.

options.text: Switch the patient to room air and recheck the saturation again later
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Removing ordered oxygen is not the nurse's decision.

questions.takeaway: Simple mask under 5: fix it.
questions.strategy: Apply the device's safety rule.

questions.stem: A patient on a nonrebreather mask has a reservoir bag that collapses completely with each breath. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Remove the reservoir bag so the patient can breathe more easily
options.rationale: Near miss concept Without the bag the device cannot deliver high concentration.

options.text: Lower the flow to 6 L/min
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lower flow empties the bag further.

options.text: Switch to a nasal cannula
options.rationale: Near miss concept A cannula gives much less oxygen.

options.text: Increase the flow until the bag stays partly inflated
options.rationale: The reservoir must stay partly inflated during inspiration. A collapsing bag means the flow is too low for the patient's demand, so the nurse increases the flow and reassesses.

questions.takeaway: Collapsing bag: raise the flow.
questions.strategy: Keep the reservoir working.

questions.stem: A patient who has used a nasal cannula for 4 days has redness behind both ears. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document it only at discharge
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Skin changes are addressed and documented now.

options.text: Remove the cannula for the rest of the shift
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Removing ordered oxygen is not appropriate.

options.text: Pad the tubing and reassess the skin regularly
options.rationale: Cannula tubing presses on the ears and nares. The nurse protects the skin with padding, checks it regularly and documents.

options.text: Tighten the tubing to stop it moving
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tightening increases pressure.

questions.takeaway: Cannula: protect the ears.
questions.strategy: Treat the pressure, keep the oxygen.

questions.stem: Match each adult vital sign to its normal range.
questions.takeaway: Adult normals: pulse 60 to 100, respirations 12 to 20, temperature 36 to 38 °C and SpO2 95 to 100%, which may be lower at baseline in chronic lung disease. 60 to 100, 12 to 20, 36 to 38, 95 to 100.
questions.strategy: Compare the number with the patient, not just with normal.

questions.stem: Match each temperature site to its key feature.

rows.text: Affected by cerumen and ear canal angle
Avoid after recent hot or cold drinks

questions.takeaway: Oral is convenient but affected by recent hot or cold intake and avoided if unconscious or mouth breathing. Tympanic is fast but affected by cerumen. Rectal is most accurate. Axillary is least accurate. Rectal most accurate, axillary least.
questions.strategy: Match each site to its main limitation.

questions.stem: Which patient should not have a rectal temperature taken?

options.text: A patient who is mouth breathing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Mouth breathing rules out an oral reading, not a rectal one.

options.text: A patient with a cold drink 5 minutes ago
options.rationale: Near miss concept Recent drinks affect oral readings.

options.text: A patient who is confused
options.rationale: Near miss concept Confusion is not a contraindication to a rectal reading.

options.text: A patient with a platelet count of 22,000
options.rationale: Rectal temperatures are avoided with low platelets or recent rectal surgery because of the risk of bleeding and injury.

questions.takeaway: Low platelets: no rectal.
questions.strategy: Ask which patient could bleed.

questions.stem: Match each description to the temperature alteration.

rows.text: Uncontrolled rise not caused by the body's set point, as in heat stroke
Elevated temperature in response to infection

questions.takeaway: Fever is a regulated rise in response to infection or inflammation. Hyperthermia is an uncontrolled rise, as in heat stroke, that the body cannot regulate. Hypothermia is a core temperature below 35 °C. Fever is regulated; hyperthermia is not.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the body set the higher temperature.

questions.stem: Select all of the situations in which an apical pulse is preferred.

options.text: Before giving certain cardiac medications
options.rationale: The apical pulse, at the 5th intercostal space midclavicular line, is used for infants, irregular rhythms and before certain cardiac drugs.

options.text: An infant
options.rationale: The apical pulse, at the 5th intercostal space midclavicular line, is used for infants, irregular rhythms and before certain cardiac drugs.

options.text: A patient with cold fingers who needs SpO2
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is an SpO2 problem, not a pulse site question.

options.text: An irregular rhythm
options.rationale: The apical pulse, at the 5th intercostal space midclavicular line, is used for infants, irregular rhythms and before certain cardiac drugs.

options.text: Checking circulation in the foot
options.rationale: Near miss concept Circulation to the foot is checked with pedal pulses.

options.text: A healthy adult with a regular radial pulse
options.rationale: Near miss concept A radial pulse is acceptable for a regular rhythm.

questions.takeaway: Apical: infants, irregular, cardiac drugs.
questions.strategy: Pick situations needing the most accurate rate.

questions.stem: A nurse finds a weak, thready radial pulse in one arm. Select all of the appropriate actions.

options.text: Recheck at the next routine vital signs only
options.rationale: Correct but premature A possible perfusion problem needs assessment now.

options.text: Check for pallor and cool skin below the weak pulse
options.rationale: Compare both sides, look for signs of poor perfusion distal to the weak pulse, check for anything constricting flow and use a Doppler to find low velocity flow.

options.text: Look for swelling or anything restricting flow
options.rationale: Compare both sides, look for signs of poor perfusion distal to the weak pulse, check for anything constricting flow and use a Doppler to find low velocity flow.

options.text: Use a Doppler if the pulse is hard to find
options.rationale: Compare both sides, look for signs of poor perfusion distal to the weak pulse, check for anything constricting flow and use a Doppler to find low velocity flow.

options.text: Document it as normal
options.rationale: Near miss concept A weak, unequal pulse is not normal.

options.text: Compare with the radial pulse in the other arm
options.rationale: Compare both sides, look for signs of poor perfusion distal to the weak pulse, check for anything constricting flow and use a Doppler to find low velocity flow.

questions.takeaway: Weak pulse: compare, look downstream, use a Doppler.
questions.strategy: Investigate before documenting.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about counting respirations.
questions.sentence: Count respirations for [[1]] (or 30 seconds times 2 if regular), ideally [[2]], and assess rate, rhythm, depth and [[3]].

options.text: 15 seconds
a full 60 seconds
2 minutes
while the patient talks
after asking the patient to breathe normally
while the patient is unaware
effort
skin color only
temperature

questions.takeaway: Patients change their breathing when they know it is being counted, so it is counted without their awareness, often right after the pulse. Rate, rhythm, depth and effort are assessed, including accessory muscle use. Count a full minute without telling the patient.
questions.strategy: Each blank stands alone.

questions.stem: Which is an early sign of hypoxia?

options.text: Restlessness
options.rationale: Restlessness and confusion are early signs because the brain is sensitive to low oxygen. Cyanosis appears late.

options.text: Clubbing of the fingers
options.rationale: Near miss concept Clubbing is a chronic sign, not an early acute one.

options.text: Bradycardia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bradycardia is a late, ominous sign.

options.text: Cyanosis of the lips
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cyanosis is a late sign.

questions.takeaway: Early hypoxia: restless and confused. Late: cyanosis.
questions.strategy: Look for the brain's first warning.

questions.stem: Classify each adult blood pressure.
questions.takeaway: Normal: under 120/80. Elevated: 120 to 129 systolic and diastolic under 80. Stage 1: 130 to 139 or 80 to 89. Stage 2: 140 or more, or 90 or more. Use the higher category when the two numbers fall in different ones. 120, 130, 140 are the systolic cutoffs.
questions.strategy: Classify by whichever number is worse.

questions.stem: Match each error to its effect on the reading.
questions.takeaway: A cuff too small or an arm below heart level reads high; a cuff too large reads low. Crossed legs, talking and no rest also raise the reading. Small cuff high, large cuff low.
questions.strategy: Most errors push the reading up.

questions.stem: Place the steps of the two step blood pressure method in order.

options.text: Wait about 30 seconds
Inflate 20 to 30 mm Hg above the estimated systolic and listen
Palpate the brachial pulse and inflate until it disappears
Deflate the cuff completely
Deflate at 2 to 3 mm Hg per second, noting the first and last sounds

questions.takeaway: Palpating first estimates the systolic and prevents missing an auscultatory gap. After deflating and waiting 30 seconds, inflate 20 to 30 above the estimate and deflate slowly. The first clear sound is the systolic; disappearance is the diastolic. Palpate, deflate, wait, inflate above, listen.
questions.strategy: Estimate before you listen.

questions.stem: Select all of the arms the nurse avoids for a blood pressure.

options.text: The dominant arm with no restrictions
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dominance alone does not rule out an arm.

options.text: An uninjured arm without devices
options.rationale: Near miss concept An uninjured arm without devices is appropriate.

options.text: An arm with a dialysis fistula
options.rationale: Cuff pressure can injure tissue or vessels and interrupt an infusion or a fistula. Avoid the mastectomy side, dialysis access, an IV, injury or a cast. The leg can be used if both arms are unavailable.

options.text: An arm in a cast
options.rationale: Cuff pressure can injure tissue or vessels and interrupt an infusion or a fistula. Avoid the mastectomy side, dialysis access, an IV, injury or a cast. The leg can be used if both arms are unavailable.

options.text: An arm with an infusing IV
options.rationale: Cuff pressure can injure tissue or vessels and interrupt an infusion or a fistula. Avoid the mastectomy side, dialysis access, an IV, injury or a cast. The leg can be used if both arms are unavailable.

options.text: The arm on the side of a mastectomy
options.rationale: Cuff pressure can injure tissue or vessels and interrupt an infusion or a fistula. Avoid the mastectomy side, dialysis access, an IV, injury or a cast. The leg can be used if both arms are unavailable.

questions.takeaway: No cuff on protected arms.
questions.strategy: Ask what the cuff could damage.

questions.stem: Select all of the factors that can cause an inaccurate SpO2 reading.

options.text: Cold extremities
options.rationale: Nail polish blocks light, poor perfusion and cold limit pulsatile flow and motion creates artifact. Assess the patient and try another site before trusting a low reading.

options.text: A warm, still finger
options.rationale: Near miss concept Warm, still fingers give the best readings.

options.text: Poor perfusion
options.rationale: Nail polish blocks light, poor perfusion and cold limit pulsatile flow and motion creates artifact. Assess the patient and try another site before trusting a low reading.

options.text: Patient movement
options.rationale: Nail polish blocks light, poor perfusion and cold limit pulsatile flow and motion creates artifact. Assess the patient and try another site before trusting a low reading.

options.text: Clean, dry skin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Clean, dry skin does not interfere.

options.text: Nail polish
options.rationale: Nail polish blocks light, poor perfusion and cold limit pulsatile flow and motion creates artifact. Assess the patient and try another site before trusting a low reading.

questions.takeaway: Polish, poor flow, cold, motion.
questions.strategy: Each factor disrupts the light or the pulse.

questions.stem: Match each PQRSTU question to its letter.

rows.text: Where is the pain, and does it travel anywhere?
What does the pain feel like?
What makes it worse or better?
When did it start, and what have you taken for it?
How would you rate it from 0 to 10?

questions.takeaway: P asks what makes it worse or better. Q asks what it feels like. R asks where and whether it radiates. S rates severity. T asks when it started and what has been tried. U asks what the patient thinks is causing it. PQRSTU walks through the pain story.
questions.strategy: Match the question to the letter's word.

questions.stem: Which trend suggests possible shock?

options.text: Temperature rising and respirations falling
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rising temperature usually raises respirations.

options.text: SpO2 rising and pain falling
options.rationale: Near miss concept Those suggest improvement.

options.text: Heart rate falling and blood pressure rising
options.rationale: Near miss concept That pattern suggests other problems, such as rising intracranial pressure.

options.text: Heart rate rising and blood pressure falling
options.rationale: In shock, the heart speeds up to compensate for falling volume or pressure. A rising heart rate with a falling blood pressure is a warning trend. Trends over time are more valuable than a single reading.

questions.takeaway: Pulse up, pressure down: shock.
questions.strategy: Read the vital signs together.

questions.stem: A nurse administers an oral analgesic at 1400. When should the nurse reassess the patient's pain?

options.text: Only if the patient reports continued pain
options.rationale: Near miss concept Makes evaluation conditional on the patient initiating it.

options.text: At 1600 with the next set of vital signs
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Attaches reassessment to a routine rather than to the drug.

options.text: Between 1415 and 1430
options.rationale: Near miss concept The intravenous window applied to an oral dose.

options.text: Between 1445 and 1500
options.rationale: Oral analgesics are reassessed at roughly 45 to 60 minutes, which is when the peak effect occurs. Intravenous doses are reassessed at roughly 15 to 30 minutes. Reassessment is what turns giving a drug into nursing, and it does not depend on the patient speaking up.

questions.takeaway: Oral 45 to 60 minutes, intravenous 15 to 30.
questions.strategy: Match the window to the route. Two options here are the correct window for a different route or no window at all.

questions.stem: Select all of the parameters the nurse monitors in a patient receiving opioids.

options.text: Bowel function and the need for a bowel regimen
options.rationale: Sedation precedes respiratory depression, so the sedation scale is the early warning and the respiratory rate is the late one. Depth and pattern matter as much as rate, because a rate of 16 that is shallow is not reassuring. Constipation is universal and prevented rather than treated. Routine serum levels and liver enzymes before every dose are not standard practice.

options.text: Oxygen saturation and, where indicated, end tidal carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Sedation precedes respiratory depression, so the sedation scale is the early warning and the respiratory rate is the late one. Depth and pattern matter as much as rate, because a rate of 16 that is shallow is not reassuring. Constipation is universal and prevented rather than treated. Routine serum levels and liver enzymes before every dose are not standard practice.

options.text: Respiratory rate, depth and pattern
options.rationale: Sedation precedes respiratory depression, so the sedation scale is the early warning and the respiratory rate is the late one. Depth and pattern matter as much as rate, because a rate of 16 that is shallow is not reassuring. Constipation is universal and prevented rather than treated. Routine serum levels and liver enzymes before every dose are not standard practice.

options.text: Serum opioid levels every shift
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Not standard monitoring; the clinical assessment is what guides care.

options.text: Liver enzymes before every dose
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Relevant in specific circumstances, not before each dose.

options.text: Level of sedation using a scale
options.rationale: Sedation precedes respiratory depression, so the sedation scale is the early warning and the respiratory rate is the late one. Depth and pattern matter as much as rate, because a rate of 16 that is shallow is not reassuring. Constipation is universal and prevented rather than treated. Routine serum levels and liver enzymes before every dose are not standard practice.

questions.takeaway: Grade the sedation. Waiting for the respiratory rate is waiting too long.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are laboratory tests that are not part of routine opioid monitoring.

questions.stem: A nurse asks a patient, "What were you doing when it started, and what makes it better or worse?" Which element of PQRST is being assessed?

options.text: Quality
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would ask what the pain feels like.

options.text: Region and radiation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would ask where it is and where it travels.

options.text: Provocation and palliation
options.rationale: P is provocation and palliation: what brings it on and what relieves it. Q is quality, in the patient's own words. R is region and radiation. S is severity on a scale. T is timing, meaning onset, duration and pattern. A full assessment also covers the effect on function, what has worked before, and the patient's own acceptable pain goal.

options.text: Timing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would ask when it started and how long it lasts.

questions.takeaway: The acceptable pain goal is the part students skip, and it is what you evaluate against.
questions.strategy: Match the question asked to the letter, not to the letter you would ask first.

questions.stem: A patient describes burning, shooting pain in both feet that is worse at night and is not relieved by the prescribed opioid. Which statement by the nurse reflects the best understanding?

options.text: This pattern suggests neuropathic pain, which often responds better to an adjuvant medication
options.rationale: Burning and shooting quality, a symmetric distribution and poor opioid response are characteristic of neuropathic pain, which typically responds to adjuvants such as gabapentin. Increasing an opioid that is not working for the mechanism adds risk without benefit.

options.text: The opioid dose is inadequate and should be increased
options.rationale: Near miss concept Escalates a drug class that does not match the mechanism.

options.text: Pain that is worse at night usually indicates a psychological component
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism A label in place of a mechanism; nocturnal worsening is typical of neuropathy.

options.text: Burning pain in both feet is an expected finding and does not require treatment
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Normalizes a treatable symptom.

questions.takeaway: The words the patient uses tell you the mechanism, and the mechanism picks the drug.
questions.strategy: When a stem gives you quality plus poor response to a class, it is asking about pain type.

questions.stem: Select all of the nursing measures that can be used alongside analgesia for postoperative pain.

options.text: Withholding analgesia until the patient demonstrates the techniques
options.rationale: Near miss concept Turns a comfort measure into a condition for treatment.

options.text: Repositioning and supporting the incision with a pillow during coughing
options.rationale: Nonpharmacologic measures work with analgesia, not instead of it. They raise the pain threshold, give the patient something to control, and reduce the dose needed. Making medication conditional on them is coercive, and waiting for pain free before moving produces the complications that immobility causes.

options.text: Guided imagery and relaxation breathing
options.rationale: Nonpharmacologic measures work with analgesia, not instead of it. They raise the pain threshold, give the patient something to control, and reduce the dose needed. Making medication conditional on them is coercive, and waiting for pain free before moving produces the complications that immobility causes.

options.text: Delaying ambulation until the patient is completely pain free
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pain free is not the goal; functional is.

options.text: Cold application to a swollen surgical site per order
options.rationale: Nonpharmacologic measures work with analgesia, not instead of it. They raise the pain threshold, give the patient something to control, and reduce the dose needed. Making medication conditional on them is coercive, and waiting for pain free before moving produces the complications that immobility causes.

options.text: Distraction with music or conversation
options.rationale: Nonpharmacologic measures work with analgesia, not instead of it. They raise the pain threshold, give the patient something to control, and reduce the dose needed. Making medication conditional on them is coercive, and waiting for pain free before moving produces the complications that immobility causes.

questions.takeaway: These are additions to analgesia, never substitutes or conditions for it.
questions.strategy: An option that makes pain relief contingent on patient behavior is wrong every time.

questions.stem: A patient's baseline blood pressure is 152/94. Today it is 104/62, with a heart rate of 112. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: A significant change from baseline
options.rationale: A 48 point drop from baseline with a fast heart rate suggests hypovolemia or another problem. The nurse compares with the baseline, assesses and reports.

options.text: An improvement in hypertension control
options.rationale: Near miss concept A drop with a rising heart rate is a concern, not improvement.

options.text: A measurement error
options.rationale: Near miss concept Assume it is real until reassessed.

options.text: A normal reading
options.rationale: Near miss concept Normal for the population is not normal for this patient.

questions.takeaway: Compare with the patient's baseline.
questions.strategy: A normal number can still be a bad change.

questions.stem: A patient's pulse oximeter reads 84%. The patient is talking comfortably, pink and breathing 16 times a minute with cold fingers. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Notify the rapid response team
options.rationale: Correct but premature Nothing suggests an emergency yet.

options.text: Document the SpO2 as 84% in the flowsheet right away
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Documenting a likely false reading misleads the team.

options.text: Apply oxygen at 10 L/min by nonrebreather
options.rationale: Correct but premature The patient shows no distress; the reading is likely false.

options.text: Warm the hand or move the probe and recheck
options.rationale: The patient's appearance does not match the number, and cold fingers cause false lows. The nurse checks the probe site, warms the hand or moves the probe and reassesses, while staying ready to treat a real low.

questions.takeaway: Treat the patient, not the monitor.
questions.strategy: When the number and the patient disagree, check the equipment.

questions.stem: A patient who received an opioid becomes restless and confused. Respirations are 26 and shallow, and SpO2 is 89%. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ask the family to sit with and calm the patient until the restlessness passes
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic The cause is likely hypoxia, not anxiety.

options.text: Help the patient into a supported sitting position and apply oxygen per order
options.rationale: New restlessness and confusion with low SpO2 are early signs of hypoxia. The nurse positions the patient upright, applies oxygen as ordered, assesses for causes and notifies the provider if it continues.

options.text: Give the next scheduled opioid dose early to settle the restlessness and pain
options.rationale: Near miss concept More opioid could worsen breathing.

options.text: Recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: Correct but premature Early hypoxia needs action now.

questions.takeaway: Restless and low SpO2: position and oxygen.
questions.strategy: Treat the early hypoxia.

questions.stem: Which patient's vital signs are most appropriate to delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: A patient whose blood pressure dropped 30 points an hour ago
options.rationale: Near miss concept An unstable patient needs the nurse.

options.text: A patient with new chest pain
options.rationale: Near miss concept New chest pain needs the nurse's assessment.

options.text: A patient who just returned from surgery
options.rationale: Near miss concept A fresh postoperative patient needs nursing assessment.

options.text: A stable patient admitted yesterday for cellulitis
options.rationale: The nurse determines the patient's status before delegating. Stable patients with predictable findings can have vital signs delegated; unstable or newly changing patients cannot.

questions.takeaway: Delegate the stable, predictable patient.
questions.strategy: Keep the unstable patients.

questions.stem: A patient one day after surgery received intravenous morphine 40 minutes ago. The patient is difficult to arouse, responds only to repeated loud verbal stimulus, and the patient's respiratory rate is 12. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document the sedation level and reassess at the next scheduled check
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Records the warning and waits for the event.

options.text: Hold further opioid doses, stimulate the patient and notify the provider
options.rationale: Sedation precedes respiratory depression, so the level of arousal is the early warning and the respiratory rate is the late one. A patient who is difficult to arouse needs the opioid held and the provider notified now. Naloxone is reserved for actual respiratory depression and reverses analgesia along with the sedation.

options.text: Administer naloxone immediately and then reassess
options.rationale: Correct but premature Skips the graded response and strips the analgesia.

options.text: Continue the current plan, because a respiratory rate of 12 is within normal limits
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Uses a normal number to override an abnormal exam.

questions.takeaway: Waiting for the respiratory rate to fall is waiting too long.
questions.strategy: The normal looking vital sign in this stem is the distractor. Grade the sedation.

questions.stem: A patient two days after abdominal surgery is laughing with visitors. When the nurse asks about pain the patient rates it 8 of 10 and says the patient cannot take a deep breath. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Treat the pain based on the patient's report
options.rationale: The patient's report is the standard, not the patient's behavior. People in severe pain distract themselves, and patients with chronic pain often stop displaying it. The functional detail in this stem matters too: inability to take a deep breath after abdominal surgery raises the risk of atelectasis and pneumonia.

options.text: Document that the patient appears comfortable and reassess later
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Charts the observation and overrides the patient.

options.text: Wait until the visitors leave and then reassess the pain
options.rationale: Correct but premature Delays treatment for a reason that has nothing to do with the patient.

options.text: Explain that the patient's behavior does not suggest severe pain and offer repositioning
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Tells the patient the pain is not what they say it is.

questions.takeaway: Behavior is not a pain scale. The report is.
questions.strategy: When a stem contrasts appearance with report, the report wins unless the patient cannot self report.

questions.stem: A patient 18 hours after surgery has received three doses of intravenous hydromorphone. The patient is now arousable only to vigorous stimulation, respirations are 8 and shallow, and the patient's oxygen saturation is 88 percent. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Give naloxone immediately before anything else
options.rationale: Correct but premature Correct drug, second action; the patient needs ventilation now and a titrated dose after.

options.text: Obtain an arterial blood gas to confirm the problem
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Confirms what you can already see.

options.text: Stimulate the patient, support breathing, give oxygen, call for help
options.rationale: Airway and breathing come before the antidote. Stimulate, open the airway, support ventilation with a bag mask if needed and get oxygen on, and call for help, all of which happens in seconds. Naloxone comes next and is given in small titrated doses, because a full dose reverses all the analgesia and can precipitate severe pain, agitation and in some patients pulmonary edema.

options.text: Hold the next dose and reassess the patient in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the response to oversedation, not to a rate of 8 with a saturation of 88.

questions.takeaway: Support the breathing first, then titrate naloxone. The antidote is not the first action.
questions.strategy: This is the item where the obviously right drug is the second step, not the first.

questions.stem: A patient's family member asks whether they can press the patient controlled analgesia button while the patient sleeps so the patient does not wake in pain. What should the nurse say?

options.text: The family member may press it once each hour if the patient's recent pain scores were high
options.rationale: Near miss concept Any proxy dosing is unsafe, at any frequency.

options.text: That is acceptable as long as the patient has given permission
options.rationale: Near miss concept Permission does not restore the safety feature.

options.text: Only the patient may press it; that is the system's safety feature
options.rationale: The system is safe because a patient who is becoming oversedated cannot press the button. Proxy dosing removes that protection, which is exactly how respiratory depression happens. Explain it kindly, because the family is trying to help, and teach them to call you instead if the pain is not controlled.

options.text: The family member should press it only at night when nurses are less available
options.rationale: Near miss concept Night is when respiratory depression is least likely to be noticed.

questions.takeaway: The patient's own hand is the safety mechanism. That is the whole design.
questions.strategy: Every option that lets someone else press it defeats the system.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic back pain is admitted. The patient is watching television and laughing with a visitor. When asked, the patient rates the pain 8 of 10 and says it is always like this. The patient's last analgesic was four hours ago and is due. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the dose but note the inconsistency between the reported pain and the observed behavior
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gives the drug and writes a note that will prime the next nurse to doubt the patient.

options.text: Discuss with the provider whether the patient's use of opioids should be reduced
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Reads normal chronic pain behavior as a reason for suspicion.

options.text: Hold the dose and document that the patient appears comfortable
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Substitutes your observation for the patient's report and withholds an ordered drug.

options.text: Give the analgesic as ordered and assess the patient's functional goal for pain
options.rationale: Patients with chronic pain stop displaying it, because a body cannot sustain pain behavior for years. The patient's report is the standard. What matters more here is the functional question: what does the patient need to be able to do, and what number lets the patient do it, because zero is usually not achievable and function is the real outcome.

questions.takeaway: People with chronic pain look normal. That is adaptation, not evidence.
questions.strategy: The behavior versus report conflict is one of the most reliably tested biases in pain management.

questions.stem: Select all of the parts of an admission assessment.

options.text: Nursing history
options.rationale: The admission assessment combines a nursing history, a behavioral assessment and a physical exam. It provides the baseline for comparing later findings.

options.text: A guess at the patient's discharge date
options.rationale: Near miss concept Discharge planning starts at admission, but a guess is not an assessment component.

options.text: Behavioral assessment
options.rationale: The admission assessment combines a nursing history, a behavioral assessment and a physical exam. It provides the baseline for comparing later findings.

options.text: A medical diagnosis made by the nurse
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Nurses do not make medical diagnoses.

options.text: Physical examination
options.rationale: The admission assessment combines a nursing history, a behavioral assessment and a physical exam. It provides the baseline for comparing later findings.

questions.takeaway: History, behavior, exam: the baseline.
questions.strategy: Pick the three data sources.

questions.stem: Place the assessment techniques in the usual order for most body systems.

options.text: Auscultation
Palpation
Inspection
Percussion

questions.takeaway: Most systems are assessed by inspection, palpation, percussion, then auscultation. The abdomen is the exception. Look, feel, tap, listen.
questions.strategy: Start with the least invasive.

questions.stem: Why is auscultation done before palpation in an abdominal assessment?

options.text: The stethoscope must warm up first
options.rationale: Near miss concept Warming the stethoscope is good practice but not the reason.

options.text: Palpation and percussion can change bowel sounds
options.rationale: Pressing and tapping stimulate the bowel and change the frequency and character of bowel sounds, so the nurse inspects and auscultates first.

options.text: Auscultation is faster than palpation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Speed is not the reason.

options.text: Palpation is too painful to do first
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pain is not the reason for the order.

questions.takeaway: Abdomen: inspect, listen, then touch.
questions.strategy: Ask what touching the abdomen changes.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about bowel sounds.
questions.sentence: Listen in each quadrant for at least [[1]], and ask about the [[2]].

options.text: 5 seconds
30 seconds
5 minutes
last bowel movement
last meal only
last shower

questions.takeaway: Bowel sounds are irregular, so the nurse listens at least 30 seconds in each quadrant and asks about the last bowel movement to match history with findings. 30 seconds per quadrant.
questions.strategy: Each blank stands alone.

questions.stem: Select all of the parts of the general survey.

options.text: Auscultation of bowel sounds
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bowel sounds belong to the abdominal assessment.

options.text: Vital signs
options.rationale: The general survey begins the review: vital signs, height and weight, behavior and appearance, and a scan of the room for hazards.

options.text: Height and weight
options.rationale: The general survey begins the review: vital signs, height and weight, behavior and appearance, and a scan of the room for hazards.

options.text: A full neurologic reflex exam
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reflexes belong to the detailed neuro exam.

options.text: A safety scan of the room
options.rationale: The general survey begins the review: vital signs, height and weight, behavior and appearance, and a scan of the room for hazards.

options.text: General behavior and appearance
options.rationale: The general survey begins the review: vital signs, height and weight, behavior and appearance, and a scan of the room for hazards.

questions.takeaway: General survey: first look and safety scan.
questions.strategy: Pick the overall impressions.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about the neurologic assessment.
questions.sentence: Alert and oriented times 4 means oriented to person, place, time and [[1]]. PERRLA means the pupils are equal, round and reactive to light and [[2]].

options.text: mood
situation
weather
accommodation
activity
alignment

questions.takeaway: Orientation x4 covers person, place, time and situation. PERRLA: pupils equal, round, reactive to light and accommodation. Person, place, time, situation.
questions.strategy: Each blank stands alone.

questions.stem: Match each normal breath sound to its description.

rows.text: Loud, high pitched, hollow, heard over the trachea
Soft, breezy, low pitched; inspiration longer than expiration

questions.takeaway: Vesicular sounds are soft and low over most of the lungs. Bronchovesicular sounds are medium over the large airways. Bronchial sounds are loud and high over the trachea. Bronchial sounds heard over the outer lung fields are abnormal. Vesicular soft, bronchial loud.
questions.strategy: Location and loudness go together.

questions.stem: Match each adventitious sound to its cause.

rows.text: Sudden reopening of alveoli; not cleared by coughing
High pitched airflow through narrowed airways
Turbulent airflow through a narrowed upper airway
Mucus or fluid in the larger airways

questions.takeaway: Crackles come from alveoli popping open and do not clear with coughing. Rhonchi come from secretions in large airways. Wheezes come from narrowed airways. A friction rub comes from inflamed pleura. Stridor comes from upper airway narrowing and is often an emergency. Stridor = upper airway emergency.
questions.strategy: Match the sound to where the air is blocked.

questions.stem: Match each auscultation site to its location.
