questions.takeaway: Aortic: 2nd right ICS. Pulmonic: 2nd left ICS. Erb point: 3rd left ICS. Tricuspid: 4th left ICS. Mitral (apical): 5th left ICS, midclavicular line. All People Enjoy Time Magazine: aortic, pulmonic, Erb, tricuspid, mitral.
questions.strategy: Move down and to the left.

questions.stem: What produces the S1 heart sound?

options.text: Blood filling the atria
options.rationale: Near miss concept Atrial filling does not make S1.

options.text: Opening of the aortic valve
options.rationale: Near miss concept Valve opening is normally silent.

options.text: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
options.rationale: S1 is the closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of systole and is loudest at the apex. S2 is the closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves.

options.text: Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is S2.

questions.takeaway: S1 mitral and tricuspid; S2 aortic and pulmonic.
questions.strategy: Lub is the AV valves.

questions.stem: Match each pitting depth to its grade.
questions.takeaway: Pitting edema is graded by depth: 1+ is 2 mm, 2+ is 4 mm, 3+ is 6 mm and 4+ is 8 mm. Each grade adds 2 mm.
questions.strategy: Count by twos.

questions.stem: Where is the dorsalis pedis pulse found?

options.text: Behind the knee
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the popliteal pulse.

options.text: On the outer side of the heel near the sole of the foot
options.rationale: Near miss concept There is no standard pulse site there.

options.text: On the top of the foot between the big and second toes
options.rationale: The dorsalis pedis is on top of the foot between the big and second toes. The posterior tibial is behind the bony bump of the inner ankle.

options.text: Behind the bony bump of the inner ankle bone
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the posterior tibial pulse.

questions.takeaway: Dorsalis pedis on top; posterior tibial behind the ankle.
questions.strategy: Match the name to the location.

questions.stem: Select all of the patient centered practices during a physical assessment.

options.text: Respect cultural beliefs about the exam
options.rationale: Use professional interpreters, ask before touching, drape and screen, and respect cultural beliefs. Communicate respect through distance, eye contact and tone.

options.text: Use a professional interpreter when English is not the primary language
options.rationale: Use professional interpreters, ask before touching, drape and screen, and respect cultural beliefs. Communicate respect through distance, eye contact and tone.

options.text: Ask a family member to interpret medical questions
options.rationale: Near miss concept Family interpreters can omit or change information and breach privacy.

options.text: Drape the patient and use the curtain
options.rationale: Use professional interpreters, ask before touching, drape and screen, and respect cultural beliefs. Communicate respect through distance, eye contact and tone.

options.text: Ask permission before touching the patient
options.rationale: Use professional interpreters, ask before touching, drape and screen, and respect cultural beliefs. Communicate respect through distance, eye contact and tone.

options.text: Expose the whole body at once to save time
options.rationale: Near miss concept Exposing only the area being examined protects privacy.

questions.takeaway: Interpreter, permission, privacy, respect.
questions.strategy: Protect dignity and accuracy.

questions.stem: A nurse begins a head to toe assessment and finds the patient struggling to breathe, using accessory muscles. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Continue the assessment in order to be thorough
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acute distress takes priority over a full exam.

options.text: Respond to the breathing problem and get vital signs
options.rationale: When a patient is in acute distress, the nurse responds immediately to the need, obtains vital signs and notifies the provider. The full assessment waits.

options.text: Complete the nursing history first so the data is in order
options.rationale: Near miss concept History can wait until the patient is stable.

options.text: Document the finding and return later
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Documenting delays care.

questions.takeaway: Distress stops the head to toe.
questions.strategy: Treat the threat first.

questions.stem: A nurse hears a high pitched, harsh sound on inspiration over the neck of a patient who was just extubated. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Recheck at the next scheduled assessment
options.rationale: Correct but premature Waiting risks airway closure.

options.text: Document normal bronchial sounds
options.rationale: Near miss concept This is stridor, not a normal bronchial sound.

options.text: Treat it as a possible emergency and get help
options.rationale: Stridor is turbulent airflow through a narrowed upper airway and is often a medical emergency. The nurse gets help immediately.

options.text: Ask the patient to cough and then recheck the sound again
options.rationale: Correct but premature Coughing does not resolve upper airway narrowing.

questions.takeaway: Stridor: get help now.
questions.strategy: Upper airway sounds are urgent.

questions.stem: A nurse hears coarse sounds over the large airways that clear after the patient coughs. What does this suggest?

options.text: Crackles from fluid that has collected in the alveoli
options.rationale: Near miss concept Crackles do not clear with coughing.

options.text: Rhonchi from secretions in the large airways
options.rationale: Rhonchi come from mucus or fluid in larger airways and often change or clear with coughing. Crackles do not clear with coughing.

options.text: Pleural friction rub
options.rationale: Near miss concept A friction rub does not clear with coughing.

options.text: Stridor
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stridor is a high pitched upper airway sound.

questions.takeaway: Clears with cough: rhonchi.
questions.strategy: Use the cough to tell them apart.

questions.stem: A newly admitted patient is too confused to answer history questions. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask family caregivers and review the record for baseline data
options.rationale: If a patient cannot provide information, the nurse seeks it from family caregivers who are present and reviews the record for baseline data.

options.text: Record that no history is available
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Other sources are available.

options.text: Wait until the patient is clear enough to answer the questions
options.rationale: Correct but premature Care cannot wait for an uncertain recovery.

options.text: Skip the history and complete it at discharge
options.rationale: Near miss concept The history is needed now to plan care.

questions.takeaway: Patient cannot answer: use family and the record.
questions.strategy: Find another source.

questions.stem: A patient has weakness in the right leg. On which side is the cane held?

options.text: The left side
options.rationale: The cane goes in the hand on the strong side and moves with the weak leg. This widens the base of support and shifts weight away from the weak leg.

options.text: Whichever hand is dominant
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dominance does not decide the side.

options.text: Alternating sides each day
options.rationale: Near miss concept Alternating gives inconsistent support.

options.text: The right side
options.rationale: Near miss concept Holding it on the weak side does not widen the base on the side that needs it.

questions.takeaway: Cane on the strong side.
questions.strategy: The cane does the job of the weak leg's partner.

questions.stem: When walking with a patient who uses a cane for left sided weakness, where does the nurse stand?

options.text: Far behind, to give the patient space
options.rationale: Near miss concept Too far away to catch a fall.

options.text: On the left side, slightly behind the patient
options.rationale: The nurse supports the weak side, slightly behind and to the side, where a fall is most likely.

options.text: On the right side, next to the cane
options.rationale: Near miss concept The cane already supports the strong side.

options.text: Directly in front, walking backward
options.rationale: Near miss concept Walking backward is unsafe for the nurse and patient.

questions.takeaway: Nurse on the weak side; cane on the strong side.
questions.strategy: Stand where the patient will fall.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about fitting a cane or walker.
questions.sentence: The handgrip should be at about the level of the [[1]], with the elbow flexed about [[2]].

options.text: wrist crease
waist
elbow
90 degrees
15 to 30 degrees
45 to 60 degrees

questions.takeaway: With the arm relaxed at the side, the handgrip sits at the wrist crease, so the elbow bends 15 to 30 degrees when the patient holds it. Wrist crease, 15 to 30 degrees.
questions.strategy: Each blank stands alone.

questions.stem: Match each patient need to the best device.

rows.text: Needs the widest base and greatest stability
Cannot bear weight on one leg after an ankle fracture
Mild balance problem needing minimal support
One sided weakness needing more support than a straight cane

questions.takeaway: A straight cane gives minimal support, a quad cane more support for one sided weakness, a walker the widest base and greatest stability, and crutches transfer weight to the arms when weight bearing is limited. More instability, bigger base.
questions.strategy: Match support to need.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct points for axillary crutch fit and use.

options.text: Weight supported through the hands
options.rationale: Crutch tips sit about 6 inches forward and lateral, the pad is 2 to 3 fingerwidths below the axilla, elbows are slightly flexed and weight goes through the hands to protect the nerves and vessels of the axilla.

options.text: Pad pressed firmly into the armpit
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pressure in the axilla injures nerves and vessels.

options.text: Elbows slightly flexed
options.rationale: Crutch tips sit about 6 inches forward and lateral, the pad is 2 to 3 fingerwidths below the axilla, elbows are slightly flexed and weight goes through the hands to protect the nerves and vessels of the axilla.

options.text: Tips about 6 inches in front of and to the side of the feet
options.rationale: Crutch tips sit about 6 inches forward and lateral, the pad is 2 to 3 fingerwidths below the axilla, elbows are slightly flexed and weight goes through the hands to protect the nerves and vessels of the axilla.

options.text: Weight supported through the axilla
options.rationale: Near miss concept Weight goes through the hands, never the armpits.

options.text: Pad 2 to 3 fingerwidths below the axilla
options.rationale: Crutch tips sit about 6 inches forward and lateral, the pad is 2 to 3 fingerwidths below the axilla, elbows are slightly flexed and weight goes through the hands to protect the nerves and vessels of the axilla.

questions.takeaway: Weight on the hands, not the armpits.
questions.strategy: Protect the axilla.

questions.stem: Which instruction is correct for walking with a walker?

options.text: Step into the walker rather than staying far behind it
options.rationale: The patient moves the walker a short distance and steps into it, staying within the base of support.

options.text: Lift the walker up off the floor and over the head when turning around
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lifting it overhead is unsafe.

options.text: Push the walker far ahead before stepping
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reaching far ahead shifts balance forward and invites a fall.

options.text: Lean on the walker with the elbows locked straight
options.rationale: Near miss concept Elbows are flexed 15 to 30 degrees.

questions.takeaway: Step into the walker.
questions.strategy: Stay inside the base of support.

questions.stem: Select all of the steps before ambulating a patient.

options.text: Ensure nonskid footwear
options.rationale: Assess first, dangle to prevent orthostatic dizziness, apply a gait belt, use nonskid footwear and clear the path.

options.text: Apply a gait belt
options.rationale: Assess first, dangle to prevent orthostatic dizziness, apply a gait belt, use nonskid footwear and clear the path.

options.text: Assess strength, balance and ability to follow directions
options.rationale: Assess first, dangle to prevent orthostatic dizziness, apply a gait belt, use nonskid footwear and clear the path.

options.text: Have the patient dangle at the bedside
options.rationale: Assess first, dangle to prevent orthostatic dizziness, apply a gait belt, use nonskid footwear and clear the path.

options.text: Walk the patient in socks for better grip
options.rationale: Near miss concept Socks are slippery; nonskid footwear is needed.

options.text: Clear clutter and wet surfaces
options.rationale: Assess first, dangle to prevent orthostatic dizziness, apply a gait belt, use nonskid footwear and clear the path.

questions.takeaway: Assess, dangle, belt, shoes, clear path.
questions.strategy: Prepare the patient and the environment.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings that tell the nurse to stop and help the patient sit during ambulation.

options.text: Diaphoresis
options.rationale: Dizziness, pallor, nausea, diaphoresis and weakness signal intolerance or low blood pressure. The nurse stops, helps the patient sit and assesses.

options.text: Dizziness
options.rationale: Dizziness, pallor, nausea, diaphoresis and weakness signal intolerance or low blood pressure. The nurse stops, helps the patient sit and assesses.

options.text: Pallor
options.rationale: Dizziness, pallor, nausea, diaphoresis and weakness signal intolerance or low blood pressure. The nurse stops, helps the patient sit and assesses.

options.text: Steady gait and normal color
options.rationale: Near miss concept A steady gait and normal color mean the patient is tolerating it.

options.text: Weakness
options.rationale: Dizziness, pallor, nausea, diaphoresis and weakness signal intolerance or low blood pressure. The nurse stops, helps the patient sit and assesses.

options.text: Nausea
options.rationale: Dizziness, pallor, nausea, diaphoresis and weakness signal intolerance or low blood pressure. The nurse stops, helps the patient sit and assesses.

questions.takeaway: Dizzy, pale, sick, sweaty, weak: stop.
questions.strategy: Watch for signs of poor perfusion.

questions.stem: Match each task to the team member who owns it.

rows.text: Reinforces safe device use and evaluates tolerance
Selects and fits the device and sets the gait pattern
Assists with routine ambulation after instruction and reports symptoms

questions.takeaway: Physical therapy assesses mobility, selects and fits the device, sets the gait pattern and trains. The nurse reinforces safe use and evaluates tolerance and safety. Assistive personnel may help with routine ambulation after assessment and instruction and report problems at once. PT fits, nurse reinforces, AP assists and reports.
questions.strategy: Match the task to the training.

questions.stem: Halfway down the hall, a patient walking with a gait belt says, "I feel dizzy," and becomes pale and sweaty. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Hurry the patient back to bed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Continuing to walk risks a fall.

options.text: Help the patient sit in a nearby chair or lower to the floor
options.rationale: Dizziness, pallor and sweating mean the patient may faint. The nurse gets the patient safely seated or eases them to the floor using the gait belt, then assesses and calls for help.

options.text: Leave the patient standing and go to get a wheelchair from the hall
options.rationale: Near miss concept Leaving the patient alone is unsafe.

options.text: Take a full set of vital signs while standing
options.rationale: Correct but premature Assessment comes after the patient is safely down.

questions.takeaway: Dizzy while walking: get the patient down safely.
questions.strategy: Safety before assessment.

questions.stem: A patient using axillary crutches reports numbness and tingling in both hands. What does the nurse assess first?

options.text: How many steps the patient takes each day
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Step count does not explain numbness.

options.text: Whether the patient drinks enough water
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Hydration does not explain this.

options.text: Whether the patient is leaning on the crutch pads with the armpits
options.rationale: Pressure in the axilla compresses the nerves that supply the arms and hands. The nurse checks how the patient bears weight and refits or reteaches so weight goes through the hands.

options.text: Whether the crutches are the right color and style for the patient's preference
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Color is irrelevant.

questions.takeaway: Numb hands on crutches: check the armpits.
questions.strategy: Link the symptom to the pressure point.

questions.stem: A patient is getting out of bed for the first time after surgery. Which task can the nurse delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: The first time out of bed, including the assessment of tolerance
options.rationale: Near miss concept The first ambulation after surgery needs the nurse's assessment.

options.text: Routine ambulation later in the day after the nurse has assessed and instructed
options.rationale: AP may assist with routine ambulation after the nurse has assessed the patient and given instructions, and they report abnormal symptoms immediately.

options.text: Choosing the patient's assistive device and fitting it to the right height for walking
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Device selection belongs to physical therapy.

options.text: Teaching the patient a new crutch gait
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Gait training belongs to physical therapy, with nurse reinforcement.

questions.takeaway: Delegate routine walks after assessment.
questions.strategy: Keep the first time and new teaching.

questions.stem: A nurse observes a patient with right leg weakness walking with a cane in the right hand. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Praise the patient for using the cane
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Praise reinforces an unsafe technique.

options.text: Teach the patient to hold the cane in the left hand
options.rationale: The cane belongs on the strong side, here the left, so it moves with the weak right leg and widens the base on that side.

options.text: Take the cane away and have the patient use a walker for safety
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing devices is a physical therapy decision.

options.text: Document that the patient walks independently
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Documenting does not correct the error.

questions.takeaway: Wrong side: reteach.
questions.strategy: Correct the technique.

questions.stem: Select all of the principles of a good bed bath.

options.text: Encourage range of motion during the bath
options.rationale: Lukewarm water and mild cleansers prevent irritation, cleanest to dirtiest prevents spreading organisms, the bath is a skin assessment, and normal range of motion is encouraged.

options.text: Use lukewarm water and a mild cleanser
options.rationale: Lukewarm water and mild cleansers prevent irritation, cleanest to dirtiest prevents spreading organisms, the bath is a skin assessment, and normal range of motion is encouraged.

options.text: Assess the skin during the bath
options.rationale: Lukewarm water and mild cleansers prevent irritation, cleanest to dirtiest prevents spreading organisms, the bath is a skin assessment, and normal range of motion is encouraged.

options.text: Scrub firmly to remove dead skin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Excessive force and friction damage skin.

options.text: Use hot water to improve circulation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hot water dries and can burn the skin.

options.text: Wash from the cleanest areas to the dirtiest
options.rationale: Lukewarm water and mild cleansers prevent irritation, cleanest to dirtiest prevents spreading organisms, the bath is a skin assessment, and normal range of motion is encouraged.

questions.takeaway: Lukewarm, gentle, clean to dirty, assess.
questions.strategy: Ask what the step protects: skin, airway, privacy or infection.

questions.stem: Why is daily 2% chlorhexidine bathing used in many hospitals?

options.text: It replaces hand hygiene for the staff caring for that patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing replaces staff hand hygiene.

options.text: It reduces skin bacteria and health care associated infections
options.rationale: CHG bathing reduces skin bacteria and lowers health care associated infections, including central line bloodstream infections and surgical site infections. Disposable CHG cloths can replace soap and water baths.

options.text: It moisturizes dry, aging skin
options.rationale: Near miss concept It is an antiseptic, not a moisturizer.

options.text: It treats fungal skin infections
options.rationale: Near miss concept It is not a treatment for fungal infections.

questions.takeaway: CHG bath: fewer infections.
questions.strategy: Pick the infection prevention purpose.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure tires quickly with activity. Which bath is most appropriate?

options.text: No bath until the patient feels stronger
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hygiene is still needed for skin integrity and comfort.

options.text: A complete bed bath done quickly
options.rationale: Near miss concept A complete bath may exhaust the patient even when rushed.

options.text: A partial bed bath
options.rationale: For patients who fatigue easily, a partial bath (face, hands, axillae, perineum and areas that need it) meets hygiene needs without exhausting them.

options.text: A shower with the patient standing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Standing increases energy demand and fall risk.

questions.takeaway: Tires easily: partial bath.
questions.strategy: Match the care to the patient's energy.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about oral care for a dependent patient.
questions.sentence: Raise the head of the bed to [[1]] to prevent [[2]], and review [[3]] before brushing.

options.text: 0 to 10 degrees
30 to 45 degrees
90 degrees with the head tilted back
aspiration
dizziness
pressure injury
the diet order only
the bowel pattern
the coagulation status and bleeding risk

questions.takeaway: Positioning the patient upright at 30 to 45 degrees prevents aspiration. Coagulation status and bleeding risk are reviewed before oral care, and the gums and mucosa are inspected for bleeding or changes. Oral care: head up, check bleeding risk.
questions.strategy: Each blank stands alone.

questions.stem: Which razor is used for a patient taking an anticoagulant?

options.text: A straight razor
options.rationale: Near miss concept A straight razor has the highest cut risk.

options.text: An electric razor
options.rationale: Patients at risk for bleeding are shaved with an electric razor to avoid cuts. Consent is obtained before cutting or shaving hair.

options.text: Any razor, if the nurse is careful
options.rationale: Near miss concept Care does not remove the risk of a blade cut.

options.text: A disposable safety razor
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blades can nick the skin and cause bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Bleeding risk: electric razor.
questions.strategy: Choose the option without a blade on the skin.

questions.stem: Select all of the patients who need more frequent perineal care.

options.text: A patient admitted for a sprained wrist only
options.rationale: Near miss concept A wrist sprain does not raise perineal infection risk.

options.text: A patient with incontinence associated dermatitis
options.rationale: Perineal care is given more often for patients at risk for infection: incontinence associated dermatitis, an indwelling catheter or recovery from rectal or genital surgery.

options.text: An independent patient with no incontinence
options.rationale: Near miss concept No added infection risk is described.

options.text: A patient with an indwelling urinary catheter
options.rationale: Perineal care is given more often for patients at risk for infection: incontinence associated dermatitis, an indwelling catheter or recovery from rectal or genital surgery.

options.text: A patient recovering from rectal surgery
options.rationale: Perineal care is given more often for patients at risk for infection: incontinence associated dermatitis, an indwelling catheter or recovery from rectal or genital surgery.

questions.takeaway: More risk, more perineal care.
questions.strategy: Pick patients with an added infection risk.

options.text: Clean with CHG or mild soap and warm water
options.rationale: Assess the meatus, clean with CHG or mild soap, clean the catheter from the meatus outward about 4 inches and avoid pulling or friction.

options.text: Assess the meatus for redness, swelling or discharge
options.rationale: Assess the meatus, clean with CHG or mild soap, clean the catheter from the meatus outward about 4 inches and avoid pulling or friction.

options.text: Pull the catheter gently to check the balloon
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pulling causes trauma at the bladder neck.

options.text: Clean the catheter from the meatus outward about 4 inches
options.rationale: Assess the meatus, clean with CHG or mild soap, clean the catheter from the meatus outward about 4 inches and avoid pulling or friction.

options.text: Avoid pulling or friction on the catheter

options.text: Clean the catheter toward the meatus
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cleaning toward the meatus brings organisms in.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct practices for an indwelling catheter drainage system.

options.text: Keep the tubing free of kinks and dependent loops
options.rationale: Below the bladder and off the floor prevents backflow and contamination. No kinks or loops keeps urine flowing. Emptying at half full and keeping the system closed prevents infection.

options.text: Hang the bag on the side rail above the bladder when moving
options.rationale: Near miss concept Above the bladder lets urine flow back.

options.text: Disconnect the tubing to empty it faster
options.rationale: Near miss concept Opening the closed system lets bacteria in.

options.text: Keep the bag below the level of the bladder
options.rationale: Below the bladder and off the floor prevents backflow and contamination. No kinks or loops keeps urine flowing. Emptying at half full and keeping the system closed prevents infection.

options.text: Keep the bag off the floor
options.rationale: Below the bladder and off the floor prevents backflow and contamination. No kinks or loops keeps urine flowing. Emptying at half full and keeping the system closed prevents infection.

options.text: Empty the bag when it is about half full
options.rationale: Below the bladder and off the floor prevents backflow and contamination. No kinks or loops keeps urine flowing. Emptying at half full and keeping the system closed prevents infection.

questions.takeaway: Below the bladder, off the floor, closed system.
questions.strategy: Gravity and a closed system prevent infection.

questions.stem: Place the steps for emptying a urinary drainage bag in order.

options.text: Close the spout and clean it with an antiseptic wipe
Open the spout and drain into a clean container without touching it
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves
Document the amount and characteristics
Note the amount, color, clarity and odor

questions.takeaway: Hand hygiene and gloves, drain without letting the spout touch the container, note the urine, close and clean the spout, return it without touching the floor, remove gloves, perform hand hygiene and document. Gloves, drain, observe, close and clean, document.
questions.strategy: Protect the spout throughout.

questions.stem: Which statement about enemas is correct?

options.text: A mineral oil enema flushes the whole colon with water
options.rationale: Near miss concept Mineral oil coats and lubricates hard stool; tap water flushes.

options.text: Enemas are only used before surgery
options.rationale: Near miss concept They also treat constipation and prepare for procedures.

options.text: Medicated enemas must be given by a nurse
options.rationale: An enema instills solution into the rectum and sigmoid colon to stimulate peristalsis. Tap water flushes the colon; mineral oil lubricates hard stool. Medicated enemas are given by a nurse.

options.text: Enemas slow peristalsis
options.rationale: Near miss concept Enemas stimulate peristalsis.

questions.takeaway: Medicated enema: nurse only.
questions.strategy: Look for the scope rule.

rows.text: Top linens pulled up to the head of the bed after discharge
Linens changed while the patient stays in bed
Top linens fanfolded for easy patient access

questions.takeaway: An occupied bed is made with the patient in it. An open bed has the top linens fanfolded, ready for a patient. A closed bed has the top linens pulled up, usually after discharge. Open ready, closed after discharge, occupied with the patient.

questions.stem: A patient with a platelet count of 18,000 needs oral care. Which approach is best?

options.text: Use a soft toothbrush or foam swab gently and watch for bleeding
options.rationale: With a very low platelet count, the nurse uses gentle tools such as a soft brush or foam swab and watches for bleeding, after reviewing bleeding risk.

options.text: Use a firm toothbrush to remove as much plaque as possible from the gums
options.rationale: Near miss concept A firm brush can injure the gums.

options.text: Skip oral care until the platelets recover
options.rationale: Near miss concept Oral hygiene is still needed to prevent infection.

options.text: Floss thoroughly between all teeth
options.rationale: Near miss concept Flossing can cause gum bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Low platelets: gentle oral care.
questions.strategy: Keep the care, change the technique.

questions.stem: A nurse finds a patient's catheter drainage bag lying on the floor and the tubing kinked under the leg. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hang the bag below the bladder off the floor and straighten the tubing
options.rationale: The bag must hang below the bladder and off the floor, with tubing free of kinks and loops, to keep urine flowing and prevent infection.

options.text: Disconnect and reconnect the tubing to reset it
options.rationale: Near miss concept Opening the closed system invites infection.

options.text: Raise the bag up onto the bed next to the patient so it stays clean and off the floor
options.rationale: Near miss concept At bed level, urine can flow back into the bladder.

options.text: Leave it, since urine is still in the bag
options.rationale: Near miss concept The floor contaminates the bag, and kinks block drainage.

questions.takeaway: Bag below the bladder, off the floor, tubing straight.
questions.strategy: Restore gravity and protect the closed system.

questions.stem: The nurse delegates a bed bath to assistive personnel for a patient at risk for pressure injury. Which instruction is most important?

options.text: Skip washing the back to save time when the patient is tired
options.rationale: Near miss concept The back and sacrum are high risk areas to inspect.

options.text: Apply powder generously to all skin folds
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heavy powder can cake and irritate skin.

options.text: Use hot water to improve the circulation to the skin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hot water dries and damages skin.

options.text: Report any red or open areas on the skin
options.rationale: The nurse assesses before and after care and gives clear direction when delegating. Asking the AP to report red or open areas makes the bath part of skin surveillance.

questions.takeaway: Delegated bath: report skin changes.
questions.strategy: Tell the AP what to watch for.
